Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to introduce this legislative measure to amend the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act. The purpose of the Bill is to ensure that the information appearing on the label of a prepackaged product is in both official languages.
To this day Consumer Packaging and Labelling Regulations 417 refer to implementation standards. As we know, however, a regulation may be amended at any time without the agreement of the House. That being so, with a view to ensuring the protection of one of the elements of Canada's linguistic duality, I thought it would be necessary to incorporate the regulations in a legislative measure.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: I am pleased to rise today to begin the second reading debate on Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada. This Bill marks an important milestone in the development of our country.

We have designed the legislation to take into account the fundamental elements of our language policy as it has evolved over the past 120 years, and to allow us to meet the changing needs of Canadian society. I am confident that this Bill is an accurate reflection of Canada's present day linguistic reality.
As indicated in its purpose clause, the primary objectives of this Bill are to ensure respect and equality of status for both official languages in federal institutions, notably with regard to the provision of services to the public; to support the development of English and French linguistic minority communities; to foster the advancement of both languages within Canadian society; and to set out the powers, the duties, and the functions of federal institutions with respect to official languages.
February 8, 1988

These objectives represent both continuity and evolution. They are consistent with the language provisions which were written into our Constitution by the Fathers of Confederation in 1867, and later supplemented by both the Official Languages Act of 1969 and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms of 1982. This Bill is a comprehensive legal document embracing all federal Government activities and provides all Canadians with concrete means by which they can affirm and protect their language rights.
The reform of the official languages policy had to be undertaken. Parliament has a duty to bring the provisions of the Official Languages Act of 1969 into line with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

This bill is also an important element in our efforts to effect national reconciliation. This step forward in the area of official languages complements the 1987 Constitutional Accord. Both are crucial to our national identity. Together, they reflect the government's commitment to preserve a fundamental characteristic of Canada, to promote the status and use of both official languages at all levels, and to enhance the vitality of Canada's official language minorities.

The renewal of our language policy is intended for all Canadians. It provides for the needs of the majorities by guaranteeing government services for them in their own language. In addition, it recognizes the aspirations of minorities, who have often expressed a desire, and rightly so, to live and prosper using their own language. This Bill reflects the open-mindedness and tolerance of Canadians in matters of language and culture. This generosity of Canadians toward each other is one of the most endearing features of our national identity.
I would now like to review some of the changes that we propose to make. With respect to the administration of justice at the federal level, we affirm equal access to the courts for all Canadians in either official language, and we specify what this entails.
The courts that are covered are the same ones as under the 1969 Act and under Section 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867, that is, courts and court-like adjudicative or quasi-judicial bodies which are created by federal law, but do not include provincial courts with federally appointed judges.
Therefore, this Bill applies to federal judicial bodies such as the Federal Court, the Tax Court of Canada, the Human Rights Tribunal, and so on. Of course, this does not mean that all federal judges have to be bilingual.
The Bill itself clearly imposes a duty on federal courts, as federal institutions, to arrange their affairs so that cases are heard in English, or in French, or in both languages, as the case may be, depending on who the parties are, by judges who are capable of functioning in English, in French, or in both languages, respectively.
Official Languages Act
To assist them in undertaking these responsibilities, the courts may make rules requiring proper notice. This has already been the practice for several years now in the Federal Court, the Tax Court, and a number of adjudicative tribunals.
Bill C-72 preserves judicial powers, privileges and immunities. Nothing takes away from a judge's right, as a "person" under Section 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867, to choose to use either English or French in court proceedings.
Clauses 15 through 18 are meant to respond to the situation revealed by the case law-where an English-speaking person in Quebec as in the MacDonald case was unable to obtain a traffic ticket in English; where French-speaking persons outside Quebec were unable to get a ticket in French such as the Bilodeau case; or appear before judges who understood directly the case that they were pleading, such as the Societe des Acadiens case. Again, however, these provisions are restricted to proceedings before Federal Courts.
When cases so require, these courts will have to assign judges who will understand directly, without relying on an interpreter, the official language in which the proceedings before them are being conducted. Of course, simultaneous interpretation will continue to be used by the courts. In addition, the federal Government will be required to use the official language chosen by the other parties in civil proceedings.

Concerning provincial courts exercising criminal jurisdiction, we will continue to co-operate with the provinces to implement the provisions of the Criminal Code regarding language of trial in all parts of the country.
The Government is already participating in a joint federal-provincial program to assist in the provision of language training for judges and in setting up bilingual court services. The purpose of these legislative and administrative measures is to ensure equal access for all Canadians to their judicial system.

Clause 87 amends the Criminal Code to spell out the rights that flow from an accused person's right to trial before a judge or judge and jury who speak the accused person's language. Some of these rights are essentially transferred from the 1969 Official Languages Act which, for example, gave the right to witnesses to use either language not only before federal courts but also before courts exercising criminal jurisdiction. The rest of the rights confirms the practice that has grown up in the provinces where Part XIV. 1 of the Criminal Code has been put in force, that is to say, use of interpreters and prosecutors who speak the accused's language, and so on.
I have indicated on different occasions that we have made substantial and significant progress on a voluntary basis in respect of introduction in a variety of provinces. As a Member

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
from Saskatchewan I should like to point out that recently my province entered into an arrangement in respect of the provision of trials for an accused in criminal proceedings in the French language as well as in the English language.
This would ensure that the language of trial provisions come into force by 1990. Since 1978, the Minister of Justice of Canada has had the power to proclaim these provisions in force in any province, following consultations in which no agreement has been reached with the provinces concerned, once two years have elapsed.
In January 1986 my predecessor, the then Minister of Justice, who is now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), put the provinces on notice publicly that he intended to consult them with a view to bringing the provisions of Part XIV. 1 into force across Canada as soon as possible. I reiterated that commitment to the Canadian Bar Association upon assuming the responsibilities of Minister of Justice.
Legal challenges to the province by province implementation have been mounted, some successfully, against the constitutionality of the scheme on the basis that it offended the equality rights provisions of the Charter. The January 1, 1990 date gives ample notice for bringing these 1978 provisions of the code fully into force and fully into compliance with the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Bill also reinforces the right of Canadians to use the official language of their choice in communicating with and receiving services from federal institutions. We are honouring the Charter by establishing constitutionally sound criteria for federal institutions regarding communications with the public and the provision of services. The new Act and the regulations under it will clearly determine, in accordance with the terms of the Charter, those offices at which there is significant demand for services in both languages and those offices whose nature makes it reasonable to provide such services.
Another important feature of the Bill relates to the languages of work in federal institutions. For the first time a federal law will spell out the right of officers and employees to use either official language while working for the institutions of Parliament and the Government of Canada. These institutions will be required to ensure that widely used work environments in the national capital and in prescribed regions are conducive to the effective use of both official languages. Elsewhere, the treatment given to the language of work must be comparable between regions where English predominates and regions where French predominates. When institutions carry out their language of work obligations, the right of members of the public to service in their language of choice will of course be respected.
In addition, I should note that it is not sufficient to foster the use of English or French within federal institutions without ensuring participation. The federal Government recognizes this requirement in its Bill. The Government is committed to seeing that English-speaking Canadians and French-speaking Canadians, without regard to their ethnic origin or first
language learned, have equal access to employment in federal institutions, and that the composition of the workforce of federal institutions tends to reflect in an equitable manner the presence of both English-speaking and French-speaking communities in Canada, taking into account the nature of the various institutions.

My colleague, the President of Treasury Board, has responsibility for the general direction and co-ordination of the policies and programs relating to the implementation of the parts of this bill concerning communications and services, language of work and full participation. Under the provisions of this bill, he will also be required to submit an annual report to Parliament on the progress achieved.

Bill C-72 reaffirms another important initiative of the Government-the enhancement of the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities of Canada and the advancement of the status and use of the official languages generally in Canadian society.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), who is present this morning, will play a major role in the implementation of this commitment. He will be responsible for co-ordinating federal efforts in this area and for co-operation with the provinces, as well as with the private and voluntary sectors. He will also ensure that his programs relating to official languages are maintained or developed. When the Bill was tabled, the Secretary of State announced that a further $25 million would be allocated over three years to improve the provision of key services at all levels of government.
The Bill specifies that the Commissioner of Official Languages will continue to ensure that the spirit and letter of the law are upheld. The Commissioner will be given more effective instruments to achieve that goal, including a timely and efficient process for handling complaints.
Indeed, it would not have sufficed to set out the rights and obligations I have mentioned in the absence of mechanisms to ensure that the law is enforced. The new Official Languages Act will therefore provide for judicial recourse after a complaint to the Commissioner. Any complainant who feels that his or her language rights have been violated or denied by a federal institution may apply to the Federal Court for such remedy as the court finds just and appropriate in the circumstances. The Commissioner of Official Languages will also be able to exercise this recourse to the court.
This outlines the three principles which have guided our reform of Canada's official languages policy and legislation and sums up the major changes. I am confident that the objectives which form the basis of this Bill will respond effectively to the needs of all Canadians and reflect the Government's commitment to equity in official language matters for all Canadians. Bill C-72 facilitates the full
February 8, 1988

participation of all Canadians in the institutions of Government. It reflects Canada's present linguistic reality in a manner which is consistent with both the Constitution and the fundamental principles of tolerance and fairness.
I believe this is a good Bill. I certainly commend it to the House for consideration and passage. This Bill is about fairness. This Bill is about equity of treatment of our fellow Canadians. This Bill is about the way in which we treat minorities in our country, and I think all of us seek to advance these principles in a tangible way. What we want in legislation is legislation that is not only sensitive but is fair to every Canadian regardless of which official language they speak.
This Bill after much consideration and deliberation attains what 1 consider to be an appropriate yet delicate balance in Canada which will serve as the threshold and the basis upon which we can move forward to reach the potential we have. I am heartened by the fact that there was very substantial and widespread consultation leading up to this legislation. The response to the Bill has, by and large, been superlative praise for the provisions of the legislation because it can now be said that the Bill does attain the elements of fairness and reasonableness which I think have to pervade everything we do concerning this matter. 1 do not consider this to be a trivial or laughing matter at all-
I am not laughing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a very important consideration with respect to which all of us in this House have a responsibility to assess and to make sure that the Bill does reflect those principles which all of us hold dear, namely, a united Canada, one which is based upon the fundamental principle of fairness.
I stand committed, the Government stands committed, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stands committed to these very important principles.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by saying that we share the Minister's view that the Bill must be generous, must be open and must provide Canada with a more up-to-date and more equitable framework for official languages.
Mr. Speaker, I am of course delighted to be taking part in this debate on Bill C-72, because it is the culmination of almost 16 years of parliamentary experience here in the Parliament of Canada and of over 12 years experience before that in education. I have always thought it would be nice to come to the House some day and say to whatever Government would be there: I think we have made progress, we have accomplished something. To us, this Bill is a charter, a road map, as it were, that will guide us in the years to come, and I am sure it will be a beneficial experience for all Canadians. I am pleased, the Liberals are pleased and the House is pleased,
Official Languages Act
and I feel the Government is to be commended for this initiative.
As 1 said earlier, we want the future to be equitable and fair, more generous and more respectful of that fundamental characteristic of Canada which is its English-French linguistic duality.
Bill C-72 fulfils the 1982 constitutional commitment and recognizes the formal commitments in the Meech Lake Accord, the legal version of which was tabled in the House and approved on October 26 last year.
This Bill is therefore in line with Canadian constitutional commitments. It defines federal objectives within the framework of new and updated legislation. The Liberals felt it was imperative to proceed as soon as possible with thorough consideration of Bill C-72 which, as we all know, has been on the Order Paper since June 25 last year.
I will not repeat the endless series of complaints, criticisms and requests for action that have been addressed to the Conservative Government for the past three and a half years. A glance at the Index of Hansard should be self-explanatory. There have been any number of questions and answers, debates and interventions. There is enough to fill a book on the vicissitudes of the language question.

This Bill has been long awaited by various Parties concerned with the issue of official languages, among others the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, the Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages and representatives of many official language minority groups.
The Official Languages Act of 1969 has become outdated. A number of problems have surfaced as a result of applying legislation on a daily basis for 19 years. Court rulings have weakened the scope of some of the statute's provisions. The constitutional context has evolved since 1969, particularly in light of the adoption of The Charter of Rights and Freedoms and its Sections 16 to 20 respecting language rights.
The Meech Lake Accord, signed by all provincial Premiers, states clearly that our fundamental characteristic is our language duality-English and French-and that all must strive to preserve this essential characteristic.
Attitudes have changed toward languages, Mr. Speaker. Our increased awareness, respect and generosity toward official language groups have been helpful. Language training programs at all levels and in all regions of our country have shown that there exists in Canada a greater understanding and acceptance of our language duality. There is a willingness to accept and appreciate la difference, be it immersion courses at the elementary level, core programming in the other language in secondary schools or language training programs in the workplace. There has developed in Canada over the last 20 years a new era of understanding.

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
There exists after all these years a generous Canadian commitment to making this country great and united. We are working toward bonding our people in respect and love rather than separating them in fear and hate.
Provisions for two official languages do not undermine the preservation and enhancement of languages other than English and French. It follows that the multicultural heritage of many Canadians is strengthened by collective respect and support for our two official languages.

Mr. Speaker, this Bill is the culmination of many years of hard work, reflection and personal experience. It is not the work of a single person or group, any more than it reflects the policy of a single Party in this House.
Bill C-72 is the outcome of a process that has kept pace with the development of this country, starting with the British North America Act and going on to include the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, the Official Languages Act 1969, the Parliamentary Resolution of June 1973, the Pepin-Robarts Commission, the Constitution Act, 1982 and most recently, the Meech Lake Accord. The situation has evolved over time, and it has been quite an experience for many of us, a rewarding and certainly an interesting experience.
Over the years Canada developed rapidly, following the industrial revolution. Urban development, reforms in education, the socio-culturai revolution and political leadership in the provinces, both federal and provincial, all these factors were instrumental in producing a strong push for change, and this could happen because of the understanding and generosity Canadians have shown with respect to our official languages.
In 1963, a Liberal Government headed by Mr. Pearson created the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, the terms of reference of which, as I think should be recalled, read in part:
"to inquire into and report upon the existing state of bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada and to recommend what steps should be taken to develop the Canadian Confederation on the basis of an equal partnership between the two founding races, taking into account the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada. "
Mr. Speaker, those terms of reference were issued in 1967 to a Royal Inquiry, and it will be remembered that this country was going through difficult times in the area of recognizing official minority language rights.
That may have been the true turning point as far as official languages were concerned, and it led us in 1969 to the proclamation of the Official Languages Act, later to the entrenchment of official languages in the 1982 Constitutional Act in 1982, and finally to the Meech Lake-Langevin Agreement recognizing the language duality as a fundamental characteristic of this country.
Further to the recommendations of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, the Liberal Government enacted in 1969, over the opposition of some Conservative Members on second
reading, the Official Languages Act. That Act gives English and French equal status, rights and privileges as official languages of Parliament and the Government of Canada.
Finally, in 1982, language rights were enshrined in the Constitution through the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Sections 16 to 24. From that point on language rights take precedence over any Acts or Regulations of the Canadian Government or provincial legislatures.
Since 1982, language rights are protected from political whims. Nonetheless, concrete steps must be taken both at the national and provincial levels to implement the broad constitutional principles. The everyday life of minority groups often has become difficult. They sometimes have gone through a very difficult stretch.
History tells us the issue of official languages requires more than political will. It also requires that aggressive administrative measures be put in place in order to ensure that the political will is converted into facts.
The 1969 legislation has served us well, but it has become outdated and it should be rejunevated and given a new impetus, because we need a modernized tool. To begin with, it should be made consistent with the new constitutional and social reality in Canada. Then the weaknesses which have to come to light after 18 years of enforcement should be corrected. For example, its primacy over other legislation has been questioned in many decisions rendered by the courts; its executory nature should be confirmed; the language of work concept should be clarified to allow the Public Service to become more efficient. Madam Speaker, I will come back to this later.
Communications with and provision of federal services to the public require clear and specific guidelines. The Canadian public is entitled to communicate in the language of their choice with federal institutions and to obtain services in that language. Under Section 20 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982), we find an important criterion which is not defined in the Charter but is stated as follows:
Any member of the public-has the right to communicate with and to receive available services from the government of Canada in English or French and has the same right with respect to any other office of any such institution where-there is a significant demand for communications with and services from that office in such a language; or due to the nature of the office, it is reasonable that communications with and services from that office be available in both English and French.
The two important terms are "significant demand" and "the nature of the office". Both terms are not defined in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Bill proposes that detailed criteria for "signifiant demand" be set by the Governor in Council. Concerning offices that because of their nature should communicate and provide services in both official languages, some are listed in the legislation and others will be designated by the Governor in Council.
February 8, 1988

I think that those clauses are fine and give the Cabinet the power to act in the national interest. If the decisions and designations are delayed, the Canadians will know that it is the Government and not the legislation that is to blame.
Mr. Speaker, the Official Languages Act has to be renewed. The time has come to restate outright the political will of this Parliament with respect to official languages. Even though attitudes have evolved, as attested by the fact that in the Meech Lake Agreement all provinces have recognized that the linguistic duality is a fundamental characteristic of Canada, it is nevertheless a fact that that evolution has not proceeded at the same pace everywhere.
The 1987 Official Languages Act is important precisely to consolidate our constitutionnal gains and to try to overcome resisters. We must give official language minorities the means to assert themselves, sometimes in spite of provincial and territorial governments.
For example, New-Brunswick has voluntarily made binding the constitutionnal clauses of 1982, but not the other provinces. As for Ontario, it has adopted Bill 8 on French services which will extend services offered to French-speaking Ontarians. At the same time, Alberta is opposed to the right to address the legislature in French, as was shown by the Piquette case.
The Piquette case is especially surpising, Madam Speaker, as Alberta had just signed the Meech Lake Accord. We would have expected more open-mindedness on the part of the Alberta Government, which should in a generous gesture toward its minority have seized the opportunity to broaden the use of French in the legislature, but this did not happen.
There is still a lot to do to ensure justice. The recent ruling of the Alberta Court of Appeal denies the right of the accused to have his trial before a judge or a judge and jury who speak his mother tongue. Bill C-72 will allow us to amend Part XIV.I of the Criminal Code, which deals with the language used in a trial, to develop a complete code of linguistic rights in criminal law and ensure the application of national standards within a prescribed period.
Madam Speaker, I remember a debate which took place in this House ten years ago when we were considering Bill C-42, whose purpose was precisely to amend Part XIV.I of the Criminal Code. It was suggested during the debate that the provinces needed some time before proclaiming the legislation and providing actual access before the courts to a judge and jury who spoke the language of the accused. It did not happen everywhere, as many provinces have not yet proclaimed that particular piece of legislation. However, Bill C-72 prescribes a specific date, 1990, which means that the provinces will now have to meet this requirement.
Concerning the administration of justice in federal courts, the Act will continue to ensure the right of everyone to use French or English for all matters brought before the federal courts. Subsection 15(1) of Bill C-72 requires every court, other than the Supreme Court of Canada, and I emphasize the
Official Languages Act
words "other than the Supreme Court of Canada", to ensure, and I quote:
-any judge or other presiding officer is able to understand the official
language or languages in which the proceedings are conducted without the
assistance of an interpreter.
Sub-section 15(2) provides for a phasing-in of this requirement to understand both official languages and sets a time limit of five years after the Act comes into force.
Madam Speaker, the Supreme Court therefore escapes entirely the requirements of Section 15. We have to wonder why the Supreme Court, the highest court in the land, should be excluded from the requirements of bilingualism.
The Bill does not require that all judges of other courts be bilingual. It does require the presiding officer at a hearing to be bilingual. With respect to the Supreme Court, for all practical purposes it would mean that the Chief Justice is bilingual. Is that expecting too much?
It seems to me that if Canadians now expect their leaders to be bilingual-Governor General, Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, and so on-are we asking for too much when we suggest that the Supreme Court of Canada Chief Justice ought to be able to follow the arguments of anglophones and francophones alike without the services of an interpreter? Madam Speaker, we will ask for explanations in committee, and we will consider the possibility of moving amendments.
The 1987 linguistic situation in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick as compared with that of Alberta underscores how differently mentalities evolve. We have, on one side, Quebec, New Brunswick and Ontario which have been generous and open to their minorities and, on the other, we witness less generous gestures such as those I just mentioned with reference to the Piquette case.
Still most people readily agree there has been great progress despite resistance fron certain quarters. The new legislation is a must if we want to continue forging ahead in terms of Canada's official languages, while at the same time contributing to bringing opponents on side and filling the gaps in the 1969 statute.

The question is sometimes asked, why this new law and why now? This revised law, Bill C-72, is much more than a cosmetic job. It is a major face-lift, major reconstructive surgery. The official languages framework will not just look better, it will feel a lot better too. It will feel a heck of a lot better than the old law. That is the main reason the Government, after 20 years of experience, after consulting thoroughly, and after inheriting a dossier which I know was well advanced, has had the courage to present this House with what I consider is a good Bill. Why this new law and why now? The best answer is found in a recent article by Mr. Stuart Beaty published in Language and Society. Mr. Beaty is an adviser for special projects in the Office of the Commissioner of Official Languages. He writes and I quote:

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
Proposals to amend the Act itself have also been presented with some regularity over the years by Members of Parliament, by all three Commissioners and by Parliament's own Joint Committee on Official Languages, which submitted 19 recommendations on this subject in 1983.
There have been differences of emphasis in each set of proposals, but there has also been a considerable consensus among them about the deficiencies of the present Act and the best ways of overcoming them. While there have been surprisingly few legal actions brought under the Act in the last 18 years, its day-by-day application had nonetheless brought to light a hard core of issues which need to be resolved.
1)	the law's relation to the fundamental political and linguistic nature of the country: its constitutional context in short;
2)	the implications of this national commitment where other sectors of Canadian society are concerned;
3)	its primacy over other federal legislation;
4)	the executory nature of the Act and the need to set out more clearly how it is to be enforced;
5)	clarification of how bilingual services are to be adjusted according to regional and other differences; this means, for instance, substituting a more workable concept for the "federal bilingual districts" which were never proclaimed;
6)	building into the Act itself the language of work and full participation objectives found in the 1973 Parliamentary Resolution;
7)	Clarifying the role of the main federal actors, including the Commissioner, in ensuring prompt and effective application of the Act.
[ Translation]
Bill C-72 is quite different from the 1969 legislation. The new measure contains a ten-point preamble which clearly defines the link between the constitutional progress achieved until now and the spirit of generosity and reform from which inspiration can be drawn when interpreting the law. We will have to be more generous and more equitable once Bill C-72 has been enacted. According to the Interpretation Act, Madam Speaker, a preamble is part and parcel of the legislation and provides an explanation concerning its purpose and scope. Through an interpretation clause, therefore, the legislator wants to make sure that the constitutional provisions and the law are at one. Is that better than having it included in the legislation? In its preamble, Bill C-72 refers to Clauses 16 to 20 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Federal Government's commitments to the protection and promotion of bilingualism and the protection of official linguistic minorities. In this sense, the Bill goes beyond the Constitutional Accord of 1987 which only recognized the Federal Government's obligation to preserve the linguistic duality.
As the House knows, Madam Speaker, I would have preferred the Accord to state that the federal government is also obliged to promote linguistic duality, but that did not happen.

As I said a few moments ago, Bill C-72 is more than a cosmetic make-up job; it is a major face-lift. In the section on the purpose of the Act we find a strong commitment to ensure respect for English and for French as the official languages of
Canada and ensure equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all federal institutions, in particular with respect to their use in parliamentary proceedings, in legislative and other instruments, in the administration of justice, in communicating with or providing services to the public and in carrying out the work of federal institutions which are defined in the Act.
Furthermore, we find that the Act will support the development of English and French minority communities and generally advance the equality of status and use of the English and French languages within Canadian society. The Act sets out the powers, duties and functions of federal institutions with respect to the official languages of Canada.

The purpose of Bill C-72 is to strengthen the Official Languages Act by ensuring equal status to French and English, by supporting the development of English and French linguistic minority communities and by clearly stating the powers, duties and functions of Federal institutions with respect to the official languages of Canada. It is unfortunate that the clause relating to the equality status of official languages and dealing with the rights under Clauses 16 to 20 of the Canadian Charter, does not emphasize their equality as languages of work and in equitable participation.
It would have been desirable to include these two issues under the "Purpose of Act" section because they are not mentioned as such in the Charter, as is the case for the language of service. It is agreed that these issues are dealt with more specifically in the Bill, but their inclusion in the "Purpose of Act" section would have given them priority status.
Bill C-72 confirms such existing principles as those calling for the provision of services to the public as well as Secretary of State programs promoting minorities. Moreover, Bill C-72 offers new elements concerning the language of work and the rule of law, subject to the provisions of the Canadian Human Rights Act. There is also the obligation for the President of the Treasury Board or any other minister designated by the Government to consult the Francophone and Anglophone minorities when drafting the regulations applicable to this legislation.
Consultation itself is not new. Madam Speaker. As far as I know, it has existed for at least 15 years. In June 1973, Mr. Trudeau, who was Prime Minister at the time, sent for the representatives of various official language minority groups to hear their views on his project to extend the national radio and television network everywhere in Canada and to make it possible for the CBC to serve all communities of more than 500 people regardless of where they lived. For that, it was necessary to develop satellite communications technology. It was a major step forward in establishing the significance and justice of our linguistic duality. It was very useful in that it forced us to develop a new technology to meet our own needs and at the same time become international leaders in the area of communications.

Bill C-72 had to reflect present realities. Thus, the Official Languages Committee that had previouly been created by an order of the House now has a legal status under an Act. Since 1969, many improvements were made, both in the administration of the Act and in the implementation of new government programs. They are part of government policy as legal requirements. Therefore, they had to be included in the Act, but they represent nothing new because the programs exist already.

the consultation process and helped prepare these amendments, and I also want to congratulate the Government once more for taking the initiative of tabling this Bill.
Bill C-72, tabled in 1987, responds to the principal recommendations of the Official Languages Committee. The new legislation includes the concept of active offer of services. In other words, public servants have a duty to invite the public to use the language of its choice. We also find the language of work concept and provisions for its application in the Public Service of Canada. The recommendation to make the legislation executory, which would create rights that would be protected by the courts, is essential if we want the law to be observed. The matter of full participation by both official language groups is also covered, as well as the issue of primacy of the legislation.
There are those who feel that the legislation's primacy is guaranteed by the very fact that Sections 16 to 20 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms were enshrined in the Constitution Act, 1982. According to this interpretation, the Charter would render invalid the provisions of any other rule of law that would be incompatible, since the Constitution is supreme. Incidentally, the Charter repeats, almost word for word, Section 2 of the Official Languages Act, 1969. Any lack of precision in the Act means that the extremely vague guarantees of Section 16(1) of the Charter will prevail.
Others feel that the Official Languages Act will always be the framework for the courts' interpretation and will enable the courts to determine the spirit and intent of the legislator. Since the Charter is rather vague, they feel it would be preferable to state precisely the spirit and the intent of the legislator by including in the legislation how its provisions are consequential on other Acts. This would provide more specific guarantees which would, furthermore, be supported by the guarantees afforded under the Charter.
Madam Speaker, I admit that I support the second option. I believe that the legislation should serve as a basis for interpreting the Constitution and that it would be more equitable to include that in the legislation.
To protect the provisions of the Official Languages Act, therefore, it becomes imperative to include a clause clearly confirming the intention of the lawmakers to place this legislation above any other Act, ordinance, decree, order, rule or regulation and confirming its supremacy over any other Act.
As a member of this House, I have introduced several private Bills calling on the House to have the Official Languages Act override any other Acts. From 1977 to 1984, I introduced a series of eight Bills with that definite purpose in mind.

I am therefore proud and happy to support this initiative. Bill C-72 ensures that if some essential provisions of this act are in conflict with other federal legislation or regulation, the act will prevail, subject only to the Canadian Human Rights Act. However, there could be problems with the drafting of the section. Indeed, Subsection 79(2) excludes explicitly the Canadian Human Rights Act and any regulation made thereunder. Well, it may happen that some provision of the Canadian Human Rights Act, such as Section 3 dealing with discrimination based on race, ethnic or national origin, or Section 7 dealing with job discrimination, or even Section 8 dealing with job applications and advertising, may come in conflict with the Official Languages Act.
The linguistic rights could in this case be weakened because of discriminatory motives, since the Canadian Human Rights Act is excluded from the overriding clause.
Moreover, the fact that Part VI of Bill C-72 is excluded from the paragraph dealing with supremacy could cause problems in the areas of equitable participation, language of work and language of service. For instance, there could be inconsistencies between the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act and those of the Official Languages Act.
As concerns administrative bilingualism, which covers the three major areas of language of service, language of work and equitable participation, Bill C-72 will first correct the obvious weaknesses of the Act in the matter of the language of work. As for the language of service, everyone knows that this means contributions of public servants who deal with the public as part of their work to serve Canadians. The obligation to provide services in the customer's own language has already been well covered, and this right is in fact guaranteed by the Constitution.
As for the language of work, this is a more complex issue, but Bill C-72 provides that English and French are the languages of work in all federal institutions and that employees have the right to use either official language.
The Government will have to ensure that the working environment allows real use of both languages; it will have to provide central services in both languages and ensure that the documentation and material used at work are available in both French and English.
There is a great variety of applications on the theme of the language of work. Which variations will be implemented under the new legislation? Will there be foot-dragging? We shall have to wait to see the administrative mechanisms implemented by Treasury Board. We all know that Treasury Board increasingly delegates its powers to the deputy ministers and that accountability often leaves much to be desired. We shall therefore have to remain vigilant to ensure an equitable and effective implementation.
In addition, there will be requirements as to the ability of supervisors and senior management to communicate and operate in both official languages.
We may wonder how this will be implemented in practice. Will there be sufficient political will to take necessary action? We may well wonder, and I have already raised this issue in the House several times as the instructions of the Treasury Board allow the deputy ministers and senior public servants to depart more easily from linguistic requirements.
Whatever the President of the Treasury Board might tell me, we all know the influence of a supervisor has over his subordinates. If he is unilingual, there will be a very strong pressure on the department to have all documents and communications in the language of the senior official. This is a fact. I am not suggesting that this senior official will force all others to use his language, I am simply saying that it is more than likely. We will need enlightened leaders who can tell the difference between authority and autocracy, while showing full respect for the linguistic rights of all Canadians.
Again I say that even with the new law, strong political will will be required to make sure it is duly enforced. We can easily live with the principles, but the administrative regulations and their implementation are something else again.
For example, the major issue of equal participation is covered under Bill C-72, to the extent that the Government will have to make sure that all Canadians, regardless of their ethnic origin or mother tongue, have equal employment and promotion opportunities in federal institutions. In addition, the staff of these institutions will have to reflect the presence in Canada of both the English and French-speaking communities.
Well, Madam Speaker, federal employees are not hired by Bill C-72, but by Treasury Board and the Public Service Commission of Canada. We will have to see to it that their hiring practices do reflect the spirit of the law. That is what is called political will.
Thanks to this legislation, individuals or groups who feel their rights have been breached will at least be entitled to legal recourse, which means they may be heard by a court and seek redress. This is an entirely new concept, Madam Speaker, and I do believe it is the essential aspect of Bill C-72, in the sense that it will give executory power under the law, the fact that an individual may appear before the court to seek justice, to seek redress.
The possibility of a legal recourse when one feels his rights have been aggrieved has been included in the legislation. So, ultimately, that could be a means of countering the bad faith on the part of a lazy administration.
Besides a recourse to the Commissioner, this Bill provides for seizing the Federal Court of a complaint six months after lodging that complaint with the Commissioner. One can proceed alone or with the help of the Commissioner.
This is an indispensable guarantee at which one can only rejoice although the process is long and costly. At least, it is there and it can be used.

Speaker, I welcome the opportunity this morning to speak to the Bill before the House, because to me, it is a very strong piece of legislation, and I say congratulations to the Government of Canada for tabling this Bill in the House.

We are not only dealing with the substance of Bill C-72, but with the direction in which I hope our country and society is headed. It is with some sadness that during recent provincial elections people in various communities were still attempting to maintain them as unilingual communities. We must get a stronger understanding of our history, as I hope Bill C-72 will help to achieve, but we must also remember that it took Canada almost 100 years to enact legislation protecting the language of both founding cultures.
Canada was established not through war but through an agreement between two colonies who wanted to establish a single country which would make them both the richer while protecting their cultural differences. Unfortunately, we too seldom teach our children the history of how these two cultures were brought together into one country and society. I believe that some of the tensions and difficulties in this country arise because that protection did not exist and different groups in areas of the country did not feel a full part of society.
Two of the most important commissions which have changed the direction and social fabric of Canada were the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, chaired by Senator Bird, and the B and B Commission chaired by Mr. Laurendeau and Mr. Dunton. The place to do that would be at committee, and I think we can come to some resolution that would make some sense.
I am pleased that this legislation is before us. We have probably taken three steps in this regard. The first step was in 1969 with the first Official Languages Act. The next step was in 1982 when once and for all the rights of both cultures and languages were recognized in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and soon we will have a very strong law to protect both languages. Certainly society will recognize the fact that it is not whether it is French or English, but it is because of French and English which gives our country its strength and beauty. As we live with this legislation it will make more sense and legislators and public servants will automatically address the delivery of their services in both languages.
Annually, since 1969, we have always looked at the report of the Official Languages Commissioner. It has had a certain amount of clout. It was always interesting to see what Departments were not doing so well and what Departments were doing better. There was a certain amount of pride when Departments did well, and it was very important. However, this Bill will no longer depend upon a review or a report. We will still be getting reports, but the Bill will put some teeth into
February 8, 1988

the legislation so that the Commissioner of Official Languages will be able to recommend and enforce. This is very important. If there is anything that is almost pathological in society today, it is the cynicism of recommendations constantly being made without the ability to enforce or implement them. Certainly we can now say with a great deal of pride that we have an official languages Bill that does not only depend upon review and reports but actually has some teeth to implement the recommendations coming from these reports. This is probably one of the most important parts of the whole Bill. As good as is any law, if it is difficult to enforce, it gets watered down or people tend to ignore it. That is not what we want.
I say on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we would like to ask for a couple of amendments at committee. They are nothing very great. It would be just to get some consensus in terms of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. Apart from that, we are very pleased to support the Bill. It is a step forward in the evolution of our country and our society. It gives me a great deal of pleasure to have been able to speak to it. It is something that has been very close to my heart. As a native Quebecer I saw a lot of discrimination happening to the majority of the community there when I was growing up. Today I see the progress which has been made, and I see people born in English Canada who are proud of the fact that they are part of a bicultural and bilingual society.
All I can say is that we have come a long way and we will still go a long way with positive evolutions in society that will give us the character and fabric of which many of us have dreamed. I think that will be a reality, and the Bill will help it happen.
Without being overly full of praise, I say that this is one time the Government has done something which we can all certainly support.

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard Grise (Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the Lion. Members for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) on raising the level of debate on the Bill before the House above any hint of political partisanship. I am sure the Government has no objection to the House adopting this Bill as soon as possible. Madam Speaker, as the Member for Chambly and as a resident of that riding since my earliest years-

I was raised in a very small community which had a few Anglophones. 1 had the opportunity to learn English at an early age and to attend a French high school where I had good English teachers, which improved my English a little. Of course, Madam Speaker, I would never say that I am as bilingual as you. I also had the opportunity to send my children to English schools. Even if we are Francophones in origin, we understand a little better the two cultures of our great country.
Official Languages Act
I am very proud to live in a part of Quebec where there is absolute co-operation between French-speaking and Englishspeaking people living in the community and in fact in the whole riding of Chambly. I am very proud to represent them, whether they are English or French.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak at the second reading stage of Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada. This Bill is an important piece of legislation which, I believe, reflects the many linguistic aspirations of French-speaking Canadians, whether they are from Acadia, Manitoba or Quebec, and of English-speaking Canadians, whether they are from Newfoundland, Quebec or Alberta.
Madam Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the Members of the Standing Committee, Members of both Chambers who worked so hard to prepare and draft this Bill, and especially the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hame-lin), who chaired the Committee for several months and the Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. St-Julien), the present joint chairman.
The House will recall that the existing Official Languages Act is 18 years old. It was necessary to amend the Act to reflect changes that have taken place in Canadian society in the last two decades and the linguistic reality of the eighties. We had to provide a modern and progressive framework for our language policy for the years to come. The Bill contains a number of new elements that are compatible with the linguistic needs of Canadians.
I think Canadians will approve of the rights conferred under this Bill and the obligations it places on federal institutions, and I am thinking of the proceedings and business of Parliament, legislative documents, the courts, communications with and services for the public, language of work, and so on. Canadians will also have access to judicial recourse when they consider they have been denied their language rights.
The concept of official languages has changed a great deal in the last 20 years. From the report of the B & B Commission to the 1969 Official Languages Act, from the entrenchment of language rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to the recognition of the Canadian linguistic duality in the Meech Lake Accord-when once more our Government and our Prime Minister, along with his provincial counterparts representing four different political parties, were able to sign this historic agreement that brings back Quebec within the Canadian constitutional family-, we went from what some consider to be a symbol to a concrete and living reality.
This Government, with its commitment to national reconciliation, started early to work for a reform of language policies in order to ensure institutional equality between English and French-speaking Canadians. In June 1987, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) introduced Bill C-72,

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
which is the cornerstone of linguistic renewal in this country. If there is a part of the Bill which reflects the Government's will to concretely and effectively improve established systems, it is the one dealing with administration of justice. In this regard, the Bill is to be considered as an extension of the rights afforded in the 1969 Act and of the basic guarantees given by the Constitution.
Madam Speaker, each and every year, during the Canada Day celebrations, we can see all over the country another concrete proof of the importance of bilingualism and national reconciliation for this Government. Since 1984, and particularly since July 1st, 1985, Quebec in particular celebrates Canada Day. Canada Day is not exclusively for the rest of Canada any more; Quebecers are also full-fledged Canadian citizens and celebrate Canada Day with as much vigor, energy and pride as Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day on June 24.
Madam Speaker, I will not repeat each component of this Bill. My colleague, the Minister of Justice, has stated them very clearly. Just let me, as Parliamentary Secretary, say a few words on language obligations imposed on federal institutions in the administration of justice as well as on this Bill's opening onto Canadian society in general.
In that important area, the new legislation proposes to implement the existing constitutional guarantees, namely, as the Supreme Court of Canada said in the decision on language rights in Manitoba, "to give French-speaking and Englishspeaking people equal access to the legislative bodies, the legislation and the courts of law."
Of course, the Bill states some obligations that already appear in the existing Official Languages Act. Thus, federal courts will still be required to hear witnesses in either of the official languages, to provide simultaneous interpretation services and to make available to the public their decisions in both official languages. However, the Bill goes even further. For the first time, a federal law will force federal courts to ensure that the judge chosen to preside at a hearing understands without the help of an interpreter the official language in which the case is being heard.
Madam Speaker, also for the first time, the Government of Canada will have to use in legal proceedings the official language selected by the other parties. Finally, under a new provision, forms that are required to be served by federal institutions must be bilingual.
With respect to provincial courts having a criminal jurisdiction, the Official Languages Act provides for some consequential amendments to the Criminal Code concerning the language in which the proceedings are carried on.
We have to remember that the Criminal Code already provides in Part XIV. 1 that any accused is entitled to be prosecuted in his own official language.
It has been noted throughout the years that the scope of that right had to be specified. The Bill provides that when a court orders that an accused is to be prosecuted before a judge or a
judge and jury who speak the official language of his choice, the accused and his lawyer will be entitled to use any official language during the proceedings; the witnesses will be entitled to testify in one of the official languages; the accused will be entitled to hear the plaintiff in the language of his choice; the courts will be required to offer simultaneous interpretation services; and finally, the file will include a copy of such interpretation.
I suggest this brief statement shows convincingly that this new legislation will enable us to make large strides in the administration of justice. I am firmly convinced of that.
I would now like to point out a significant provision of this Bill which shows the innovating nature of the linguistic renewal undertaken by the Government and its desire to open up the Canadian society.
Once again, Madam Speaker, I refer to the Meech Lake agreement concluded by our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) which has allowed the Canadian people to realize that we are a society unrivalled throughout the world. Canadians are unique.
As I said, the Meech Lake agreement undoutedly shows the interest shown by the Government to allow the Canadian community to become more open.
Madam Speaker, the enforcement of the legislation is not merely restricted to federal institutions. It has a wider scope since it attempts-and I insist on that term-to involve Canadians generally. Thus, it sets forth the Government's commitment to promote full recognition and use of French and English in the Canadian society, to encourage the development of French and English minorities in Canada, with as much equity and equality as must be deserved.
The Bill had surely to provide for means of carrying out those commitments. So the Governement, through the Secretary of State, intends to co-operate with the provinces, and the private and volunteer sectors to pursue those various interests. The Secretary of State will also have to attend to the continuation and development of programs relating to the official languages. The Government's policy in that area is clear: it seeks to foster recognition and use of as well as training in the official languages, everywhere in Canada.
Madam Speaker, the Official Languages Bill is a complete measure in that it makes linguistic duality meaningful. It covers the most important aspects of the linguistic field and gives them a strong and durable basis in law. It proves the very strong will of the Government of truly and really reforming its language policy. It fits in with our efforts to achieve national reconciliation. In that sense, it complements the historical Meech Lake Accord. In short, Madam Speaker, it has all the necessary elements to fulfill everybody's aspirations and expectations in that area. So, as a Progressive Conservative Member and as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister, I am very proud of the contents and scope of this Bill, and I hope it will soon be part of our federal statutes.
February 8, 1988

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO HARMONIZE CANADIAN AND AMERICAN LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in its haste to get a trade deal with the United States, the Government neglected to examine possible environmental consequences. The Mining Association of Canada said recently that it favours a "harmonization" of environmental law on both sides of the border so as to achieve "a level playing field" between environmental requirements and costs to industry.
It is fair to say that Canadians would support this concept only if standards are equalized to the higher, not the lower standards, so as to reflect the growing concern of both Canadians and Americans for more stringent environmental protection. But the Government did not address this issue when negotiating the sale of Canada.
If any harmonization of environmental standards to keep industry on both sides of the border on a level playing field is to be made, it must be done with improved environmental protection as the priority. By its own admission, the Government has not studied possible environmental impacts of the trade deal. Thus, the Government has failed to live up to its commitment to the Brundtland Commission report. What a sham!

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF U.S. WHEAT ASSOCIATIONS
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF U.S. WHEAT ASSOCIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian critics of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement in their overblown rhetoric claim that the Canadian Wheat board is gone, the family farm has been sold, and other like nonsense. Let us examine the American viewpoint regarding these same provisions.
A delegate to the National Association of U.S. Wheat Growers said: "We got shafted by Canada. We want fair trade, not free trade". The Association President, James Miller, stated: "Canada came out the clear winner in the FTA
because it will gain access to the huge U.S. market without giving anything in return".
Winston Wilson, President of the U. S. Wheat Association, stated: "We got our pants taken off on this one. We can't afford any more agreements of this type. We can't see the rights of our producers sold off. Canadians can sell all the wheat they want to us but we can't ship any back".
This is the other side of the coin. These are the comments of leaders of the United States wheat growing groups. Can it be that maybe, just maybe, our negotiators did an outstanding job of safeguarding the interests of Canada's wheat producers?

Mr. Speaker, thousands of Principal Group investors throughout Canada are angry. They are angry at this Government that promised them over eight months ago that it would soon be completing its investigation into possible misleading representations made to investors by the Principal Group.
Principal Group investors, many of whom lost their entire life savings, are demanding to know why it has taken the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs over 240 days to complete its investigation. On August 12, 1987, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) assured us that he was "looking into" allegations of misrepresentation. On August 13, 1987, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) said that his Department was "attaching high priority to this matter". On August 26 the same Minister said in this House that the investigation would be completed by the end of August. The Minister was later criticized by a bureaucrat in his own Department for going "a little too far".
Eight months later, despite all this talk of action, the investigation is still not completed and thousands of investors are demanding to know why.

subtopic: CONDITION OF SCHOOL IN FORT ALBANY ON JAMES BAY
CONDITION OF SCHOOL IN FORT ALBANY ON JAMES BAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Fort Albany is a small Indian community on the western shore of James Bay. There are 130 children, from kindergarten to grade eight, who attend the local school. Their school is a fire trap.
The school's fire hazards were brought to the attention of the Department of Indian Affairs in 1986, and again in 1987, with little response. A recent evaluation by an architectural firm from Winnipeg states that the fire detection, fire alarm and fire-fighting systems are completely inadequate. The firm recommends closing the school immediately. The firm states: "Without over-emphasizing the situation, we suggest that the lives of the children are hanging in the balance".
The Minister must move quickly to make this school safe from the threat of fire. Plans for the construction of a new school, scheduled for completion in four years, must be accelerated. Prompt action now can prevent a disaster.

subtopic: NORTHERN TELECOM-OPENING OF NEW ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY CENTRE IN NEPEAN
NORTHERN TELECOM-OPENING OF NEW ADVANCED TECHNOLOGY CENTRE IN NEPEAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday in Nepean-Carleton, the Hon. Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) opened Northern Telecom's new Advanced Semi Conductor Technology Centre built at a cost of $106 million. This is one of the most significant high-technology investments made by the private sector in Canada in the last decade.
In addition, Northern Telecom's research and operating expenses related to the centre will exceed $205 million between 1986 and 1990.
Northern Telecom is the world's leading supplier of fully digital telecommunications systems and the fourth largest manufacturer of telecommunications systems in the world. Its goal is to achieve world leadership in telecommunications by the year 2000. The company chose Canada for this major
investment because of availability of skilled personnel, enhanced trading relations with the U.S., and a favourable tax environment.
Friday was a day to celebrate, in both Nepean-Carleton and Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the violence in the Middle East has left three more dead and scores injured. While the Israeli Government seeks control through beatings and killings, the persistent resistance of Palestinian youths attests to the bankruptcy of this policy. Until now the Canadian Government has failed either to issue a diplomatic protest or ask the Israelis to show restraint.
The Israelis and the world now know that the Palestinian call for a homeland demands an urgent response or the Middle East will plunge into dangerous and violent anarchy which will threaten not only the existence of Israel, but world peace.
A long-term solution must be found and an international peace conference will provide a means. More than once the opportunity to resolve the Palestinian problem has been lost because Governments dithered. It is imperative that we do not allow this to happen again. I therefore call upon the Canadian Government to state its support for such a conference and commit itself to working towards its accomplishment with the urgency the situation demands. If this effort is made, perhaps some good can yet come from this turmoil.

Mr. Speaker, the House is the only institution in Canada where Members can exercise complete freedom of expression without consequence. This intrinsic right, however, entails a heavy burden of responsibility. By our actions we set the moral agenda for present and future generations. Recent events in this House are reason to examine this right more closely.
As a Member who was born and spent the early portion of his life in Holland, I am familiar with the rules and regulations of European Parliaments. When Members in those democracies comment on an event involving individuals, they must be certain of the facts before any names are used. Innuendo, circumstance, and partial facts are not allowed. That protects
February 8, 1988

individuals as well as the integrity of Parliament and its Members.
A few weeks ago the Leader of the Socialist Party of Canada underscored this point when, using a newspaper article as his source, he accused an innocent person of being a Palestinian terrorist. Freedom of expression means honour, integrity, and responsibility. If we follow these ideals, then no one will be hurt.

subtopic: CANADA SPACE AGENCY-DELAY IN DECIDING LOCATION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADA SPACE AGENCY-DELAY IN DECIDING LOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again Canada's space agency has been launched into the world of publicity, but not to the stars and not into orbit. Once again the Government's launch was aborted, and once again its lack of leadership has hit the news. This time it is the frustrated former head of the agency who resigned because of the Conservatives' inertia and inability to take a decision on whether the agency's headquarters should be in Ottawa or Montreal. We have been waiting more than 16 months for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to make up his mind, and we are still waiting today.
The Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) said the delay had put a lot of extra pressure on Art Collin. More than six months ago the Minister asked the Prime Minister to make a quick decision, and Mr. Ken Lewis, head of the Canadian Aerospace Industries Association, said Canadians are the victims of the space agency delay. If the Government cannot make a decision, who the heck can? Let us have a decision on the space agency as soon as possible.

subtopic: NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF MILITARY BASE IN NANISIVIK
NORTHWEST TERRITORIES-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF MILITARY BASE IN NANISIVIK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) announced last week the establishment of a permanent military base in Nanisivik, Northwest Territories. The Minister promised there would be consultation on the cultural, social, and environmental impacts of this project.
The Government does not have a good record of listening to northerners. The concerns of the Innuit with regard to low level military flights, and of the residents of Cold Lake, Alberta, with regard to Cruise missile testing, have fallen on deaf ears.
I call on the Minister to set out a specific timetable for the consultation process that will take place with groups such as the territorial Government, local communities-particularly those of Nanisivik and Arctic Bay-environmental groups, and other interested groups, and to ensure that the current land claims negotiations between the Tungavik Federation of Nunavit and the federal Government will be respected.
Further, the Minister must ensure that northerners benefit from any development in the North. I call upon the Minister of National Defence to guarantee that skilled job opportunities with commensurate training will be available to the people in whose area this project is built.

Mr. Speaker, last week we witnessed the NDP's dilemma of whether to reject the Party's longstanding policy to pull Canada out of NATO. While anxiously awaiting the result of this battle between ideology and pragmatism, we witness the now true colours of the Liberal Party as articulated this weekend by their Leader (Mr. Turner).
After some 20 years of neglecting our Armed Forces and of not pulling our weight in NATO, we see that the Liberals would further weaken our already rusty Navy while at the same time threaten our traditional freedoms and values by planning to abandon the NATO Alliance.

February 8, 1988
Oral Questions
The Liberals plan to demilitarize the Arctic, yet the Soviet Union has some 200 nuclear powered submarines, with a new one off the assembly line every five weeks. The Liberals plan to discontinue Cruise missile testing, while the Soviet Union continues to fly simulated attacks on the North American continent with their Cruise missile carriers, the Bear H Bombers.
During the last election campaign we found that the Liberals turned to Washington for their foreign and defence policy. In an attempt to swing their Party to the left are they now seeking their policy from Moscow?
Now is the time for solidarity in the NATO alliance, not a time to grab at superficially attractive but substantially inadequate measures.

maintopic: CALL FOR LABELLING OF FAST FOODS
CALL FOR LABELLING OF FAST FOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the saddest moment I have experienced as a Member of Parliament was when I had a lady in my office last December whose son had died after eating a fast-food apple turnover at Arby's. She cried in my office and said that he died in her husband's arms and he did not even have a chance to wake up. He knew that he had a problem with the food but, unfortunately, the Government has not required labelling of fast foods.
At the time I was so moved that, rather than making a partisan issue of it, I spoke to the Minister directly and asked whether there was something we could do to the Food and Drugs Act to prevent this kind of tragedy from occurring again. I waited some time and nothing was forthcoming. In mid-January I made plans to introduce a Private Members' Bill by seeking legal drafting. 1 have been waiting for that.
In the meantime another young woman has died. How many young people in the prime of their lives have to be snatched away before we in fact take some action with respect to labelling of fast foods? McDonald's has money for packaging to sell the clowns and the sizzle. Why can it not simply mark what is included in fast foods in order to prevent the senseless deaths and tragedies that we saw recently in Ottawa, and before that in the city of Burlington?
I ask the Minister to support a request I will be making tonight before the Committee on National Health and Welfare to have the Government move with regulations on fast food labelling.

Since Section 24 of the Prime Minister's conflict of interest guidelines requires all members of the Cabinet, including the Prime Minister, to register "all direct and contingent liabilities", why did the Prime Minister not act in compliance with this section by registering the moneys that he received from the PC Canada Fund?

subsubtopic: PC CANADA FUND-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:

subsubtopic: PC CANADA FUND-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES

subsubtopic: PC CANADA FUND-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES

The answer is that it was not either/or. The answer is that it was neither.

Canada Fund since they were first mentioned publicly and at no time have I or my predecessor or anyone else considered them to be related in any way to the Code.

subsubtopic: PC CANADA FUND-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I asked him that particularly in light of the fact that the same gentleman to whom he referred, prior to the weekend indicated in his view, in terms that we all understand, that money obtained under those circumstances did indeed constitute a liability. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister, I am sure, will have noted that various Members of this House, particularly from my Party, as well as government Members and the Premier of Quebec, last week called upon the Government to institute a lower interest rate policy. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF LOWER INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think what Mr. Bourassa has said in terms of the over-all desire for increased economic growth is something which this Government shares and has demonstrated with the policies we have followed and a broad range of things we have done over the last three and a half years.
What I have made very clear, and I will state quite clearly in the House today, is that we are in support of the monetary policy that has been conducted by the Bank of Canada.
I want to draw to the attention of the Member that in previous times, particularly in the 1970s when inflationary pressures were ignored, this led to considerable economic problems which took a long time to work their way out of the system. It is important to head these inflationary problems off in their earliest stages, rather than letting them develop to the magnitude which they did before.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think the Hon. Member has to cast his mind farther afield than on just one element of economic policy. What has produced the good economic results in Canada has been a range of economic initiatives taken by the Government.
If I may quote Peter Martin, chief economist for the investment dealers McLeod, Young, Weir, described in The Gazette as an influential voice in the financial community in Canada, he said: "They have had a fabulous economic policy, the best economic performance in Canada's history and an extremely good fiscal policy".
That is what we are standing on. We have followed a range of policies that were first enunciated in September, 1984. The over-all result is the creation of over 1,150,000 jobs, an economic growth in Canada that is best of the G-7 countries, an employment growth in Canada that is best of the major industrialized countries, and an inflation rate that is stable, but on the high side in relation to Japan, Germany and France. It is that inflation rate that we would like to see down a little bit further to improve our competitive position and to improve the job-creating performance that we have today.

Privilege is a time-honoured tradition in this House, and I think Joseph Maingot's book, Parliamentary Privilege in Canada, has for many of us been the definitive work on privilege in the House of Commons. Those privileges can be breached in a general way when Members or the press or anyone else shows contempt for the Chamber. It can also be argued as to what constitutes contempt. I think it can also be corrected if the record is corrected by the Hon. Member who made the statement. I am referring to statements made in this House by the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) as shown on page 12672 of Hansard of Friday, February 5. In his opening statement the Hon. Member said:

morning-
