The Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques was and is a member of the committee and he sat through two very traumatic hearings on Wednesday and Thursday of last week, February 3 and February 4, in which matters related to the Elections Commissioner, evidence collected by the RCMP, and conclusions reached by the Commissioner, were the subject of some five hours of testimony. February 8, 1988

February 8, 1988

I suggest it is wrong for the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to try to place before the House his confused interpretation of what transpired at committee hearings and allege that I should have known some of the things that happened in committee which would have prevented me from asking my question. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to thank my colleague for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy) for his interest in the official languages. First, as concerns the judges of a federal court, whether in Alberta or in another province, the important thing is to be able to provide judicial services in the language of choice when it is requested. This does not mean that we have to require that all judges of all federal courts throughout the province be perfectly bilingual.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-72 states that when the accused in a trial requests to be heard in French, he be given a Frenchspeaking or at least a bilingual judge, and that the judge be able to hear the accused in his mother tongue, whether English or French.
The Bill will certainly not require that all federal court judges in Alberta be bilingual. That is not the case. However, Alberta courts must be able to provide services to the accused in either official language, whether French or English. I can tell the Hon. Member for Calgary East that, in every province, the Department of Justice and the courts can now provide such services.
Official Languages Act
As for the second question about the language of work, especially as concerns supervisors and managers, this provision obviously applies to the language of work of the employees at a given office in a given location, not to the whole country.
If in St. John's, Newfoundland, there is a Federal National Revenue office where most of the employees are Englishspeaking with only one Francophone or bilingual employee, it is clear that English will be the language of work. It would not be administratively possible to demand, just because there is a bilingual or Francophone employee on the premises ... The same should apply in the various regions of Quebec, but not in Montreal, because Montreal, just as the National Capital Region, has been designated as a bilingual area. As far as the language of work is concerned, however, one should be able to function in the language used by the majority of the employees.

On the other hand, the 60 per cent of Anglophones in the constituency, and here 1 include people whose mother tongue is English, and those who
have another mother tongue but who have opted for English as their official language in Canada, constitute 60 per cent of the population. Therefore, they belong to the majority in Canada and in North America, but are a minority in Quebec.
Because of the strong presence of both language minorities in the constituency, I am very pleased to support this Bill which attempts to strengthen minority language rights in Canada under federal jurisdiction. In addition to strengthening minority language rights under federal jurisdiction, the Bill also has provisions to encourage improvement in language rights at the provincial level and in the private sector.
As the Minister stated this morning, this Bill is a result of wide and long consultation. As a member of the Official Languages Committee in Parliament since 1979, I wish to inform the House that over the years we have held hearings with respect to the Law and have been able to identify weaknesses and loopholes in it. Over those years we have made recommendations in order to strengthen the Law. Now a large number of those recommendations have been brought together and have been incorporated in the Bill.
What then does the Bill say? Well, the Bill deals with improvements with respect to the two official languages in Parliament, in the courts of Canada, in government institutions, with respect to the right of the public to communicate with the Government in the Public Service, and with respect to the Official Languages Commissioner. In all those areas improvements are recommended. I wish to refer to a few sections of the Bill in particular because I think they are extremely important.
In the preamble of the Bill one of the paragraphs states:
AND WHEREAS the Government of Canada is committed to enhancing the vitality and supporting the development of English and French linguistic minority communities, as an integral part of the two official language communities of Canada-
A further paragraph states:
AND WHEREAS the Government of Canada is committed to cooperating with provincial governments and their institutions to support the development of English and French linguistic minority communities, to provide services in both English and French, to respect the constitutional guarantees of minority language educational rights and to enhance opportunities for all to learn both English and French.
Those two paragraphs in the preamble are extremely important because they point to new ground. That new ground is spelled out in greater detail, for example, in Clause 38. I refer to the following clause because I think it is extremely important. It states:
38(1) The Government of Canada is committed to ensuring that
(a)	English-speaking Canadians and French-speaking Canadians, without regard to their ethnic origin or first language learned, have equal access to appointment and advancement in federal institutions; and
(b)	the composition of the work-force of federal institutions tends to reflect the presence of both the official language communities of Canada-
That is a very important clause. It puts into law some of the policies that Governments from both the Liberal Party and the
February 8, 1988

Conservative Party have been attempting to enforce for years. Similar provisions are found in Clause 40 of the same Bill.
Another clause that I find extremely good and useful is Clause 75 which provides for remedies when a person's language rights are violated. Under the present Official Languages Act if a person thought that his or her rights were violated, he or she could make a complaint to the Language Commissioner who is an ombudsman for language rights. They could make a complaint to that person and the commissioner would investigate the complaint and make a report. It would be up to the Minister or the Government to take action on that report. That is all very good. But now in Clause 75 we have provided for a remedy before the courts, in addition to the remedy before the commissioner. These improvements in the law are important.
While it is a new Bill, this Bill constitutes a series of amendments to the Official Languages Act of 1969, a law that was passed in the early Government of Mr. Trudeau, but which was based on the royal commission report of 1963, a royal commission on the official languages in Canada established by the former Prime Minister, Lester B. Pearson. I had the good fortune to serve on the parliamentary committee in 1968-69 which dealt with that legislation. Therefore, I have a very real interest in it.
This legislation also builds on the constitutional provisions with respect to language rights that we find in our Constitution Act, 1867, and in our Constitution Act, 1982. In the Constitution Act, 1867 there is Section 133 which guarantees the right of people to use the French or the English language before the Parliament and courts of Canada, and before the Legislative Assembly and courts of Quebec. That was the only provision in the Constitution Act, 1867 with respect to language rights.
However, in the 1982 Constitution Act, there are Sections 16 to 22 which entrench very specific language rights for institutions under the federal Government and institutions under the New Brunswick Government. There is a paragraph in those sections that allows any other province to opt in to those constitutional provisions. Of course we are always hopeful that other provinces will do so. Recently the Ontario Government has taken some initiatives to further minority language rights. We hope that they will opt in fully to these provisions in due course.
Also in the Constitution Act, 1982 we have Section 23 which guarantees minority language rights in education to the linguistic minorities throughout Canada. This applies to all provinces, with one exception which 1 will mention in a few minutes.
The legislation strengthens some other measures as well. Over the last few years we have introduced a court challenges program by which the Government helps individuals to finance their court cases when they believe that their language rights under the Constitution have been violated. A number of cases has been financed by the Government under that program. It is a good program. It can always do with improvement, but it is a good one.
Official Languages Act
We also have two other government programs to assist with minority language education. There is the minority language education program whereby the federal Government gives money to the provinces to assist with minority language education. We have another program to help provinces introduce programs for second language education.
All these things move in the same direction-toward greater assistance and help for minority language groups in Canada.
Many Canadians might ask how Bill C-72, which is before us, relates to the Meech Lake Accord, in particular to its language provisions. As I stated in the debate on the Meech Lake Accord, there were parts of the accord which we in this Party did not like and tried to amend. The amendments were defeated, but on balance we accepted the accord and voted for it. I want to make it clear that in my opinion and in the opinion of most people in my Party, the Meech Lake Accord did not reduce minority language rights; it did not reduce minority language rights. If anything, it affirmed and added to minority language rights.
A good number of people, some of whom are in my own constituency, will argue that the Meech Lake Accord drastically reduced minority language rights for Anglophones and in fact even eliminated them. That is complete nonsense. The Meech Lake Accord did not take away any of the rights entrenched in the Constitution under the Constitution Act, 1867, that is, Article 133. It did not reduce or take away any of the language rights in the Constitution Act, 1982, the ones to which I just referred, Sections 16 to 22 and Section 23. It did not reduce or touch those articles in any way whatsoever.
What in fact it did, if we read the Meech Lake Accord closely, was to add some new provisions recognizing the linguistic minority communities in Canada. Because this is such an issue, I think I had better refer to it once again. It goes hand in glove with the provisions of the Bill before us.
Those who will argue that the Meech Lake Accord took away or reduced minority language rights-and in particular in my case they refer to anglophone rights in Quebec-the only evidence they will give to support their argument is that part of the Meech Lake Accord which recognizes Quebec as a distinct society within Canada. They say that that provision will harm or reduce the rights of Anglophones in Quebec. I do not know how they come to that conclusion, because there is no definition of a distinct society and there is no provision to indicate that it will harm or hurt other rights.
However, there is a provision in another subsection of the same clause which recognizes the fundamental characteristic of Canada. That clause says that the Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada and Englishspeaking Canadians concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada. In the very next paragraph it says that the role of Canada and provincial legislatures, and that includes Quebec, is to preserve that fundamental characteristic of Canada.

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
In other words, by the IMeech Lake Accord, the Government of Canada and the Governments of the provinces including Quebec must preserve this fundamental characteristic of Canada which includes the English-speaking factor in Quebec. I do not know how those who argue that the accord does away with or reduces Anglophone rights in Quebec can ignore that particular paragraph.
Unfortunately this paragraph has been referred to as the "distinct society" paragraph, but some learned jurists have suggested that it should be called the "D and D" paragraph, meaning the distinct society and duality paragraph because it does both things. It recognizes the distinct society of Quebec, but it also says that duality, the English and French-speaking minorities in Quebec and outside Quebec, must be preserved by the Governments of Canada and of the provinces.
That is a new protection for language rights in Canada. I do not know how those who argue the way my learned colleague from Westmount (Mr. Johnston) does, can ignore the paragraph to which I just referred.
I have challenged those people to show me anywhere in the Meech Lake Accord provisions which would reduce or eliminate Anglophone rights in Quebec or francophone rights outside Quebec. 1 have challenged them to do that, and I have not had one person come before me who has been able to do so.
I also believe that those who argue in that way are making a serious mistake because by undermining or making little of the duality clause they may be hurting their case in years to come when they would want to use the clause to protect their rights before the courts. 1 can see the day coming when a provincial Government, as has happened in the past, will take steps through ordinary legislation to reduce Anglophone rights in the Province of Quebec. Those who are harmed may want to go to court and say that according to the Meech Lake Accord the Government of Quebec is to protect the fundamental characteristic of Canada, which includes the English-speaking community in Quebec, and that therefore they want this harmful or destructive legislation overturned. They will want to use it, and they should give it a fuller interpretation rather than ignore it as some have been doing today. This does not say that the provisions of the Meech Lake Accord could not be clearer and stronger. Of course they could be clearer and stronger. The fact of the matter is that they do not specifically reduce or eliminate language rights at all.
Having said that, this is not to say that there have not been attacks on English-speaking minority rights in the Province of Quebec. Of course there have been such attacks, and they have been overwhelmingly carried out by provincial Governments, in particular by certain clauses of Quebec Bill 101. By the way, the Quebec Governments which introduced that Bill did it without the help of the Meech Lake Accord. When a Government wants to act in the way they acted in respect of Bill 101 and wants to attack language rights, it does not need a Meech Lake Accord to do it. They did not need it in the past. There are still several oppressive sections in Bill 101 in respect of language rights.
1 can accept parts of that law which are meant to protect and promote the French language, to make sure that it survives, but I cannot accept articles in Quebec Bill 101 which outlaw and suppress the English language which existed in that province going back to the 17th century and which, by the way, in parts of the province was the first European language there. We all know that both the French and English speaking communities only came in the 17th century. There were aboriginal languages long before either the French or the English came. In any case, the English language was in parts of Quebec going back to the 17th century. It is a complete travesty of justice to try to eliminate those language rights.
Of course, the Supreme Court of Canada has already struck down several provisions of Quebec's Bill 101. It has struck down the provision that would have eliminated English in the courts and in the legislature of Quebec. The Supreme Court of Canada has also struck down the provision which would have insisted on the Quebec clause with respect to education rather than the Canada clause. Both the Superior Court of Quebec and the Quebec Court of Appeal have struck down the provisions eliminating English on commercial signs, and that case is now before the Supreme Court for which we are awaiting judgment.
1 must say that with respect to the signs law, I am extremely disillusioned and disappointed with the present policies of the Quebec Government. Premier Bourassa in the election of 1985 very clearly said that he would modify Bill 101, the French langauge Charter, to allow the use of English on commercial signs in Quebec. Not only did he promise that in the election but it was part of the Liberal Party platform in Quebec. The polls in Quebec overwhelming supported that kind of action. Francophones in Quebec overwhelmingly felt that Anglophones had the right to put English on signs in addition to French.
One cannot understand what Mr. Bourassa and the Quebec Government is afraid of. Do they think that the 95 per cent Francophone population of Quebec will flood the province with bilingual signs? Do they think we are going to see bilingual signs in Lac-St-Jean, Abitibi, Gaspe, the Beauce, Champlain and so on and so on? Only 5 per cent of the province is English speaking. The English speaking minority is limited mostly to Montreal and the Eastern Townships, in the Gaspe to a certain extent, and up here near Ottawa. They are not asking to be allowed to have unilingual English signs. What they are asking is that they have the right to put English on signs in addition to French. They admit and accept that French must be required on all signs in the province but they are saying that when certain individuals want to add English they should have the right to do so. That is a long standing right and it is wrong for the province to take that right away and it is particularly wrong for the Premier of the province to welsh on promises that he made during the election campaign with respect to those rights.
February 8, 1988

When the Constitution Act of 1982 was before this House I, of course, supported it.

speechtext: There is only one minute remaining for the Hon. Member to wrap up his speech.

I am sorry I did not have my attention on the Chair, Madam Speaker, and did not see your signals.
The Bill before this House is an excellent Bill. It moves to protect English and French speaking language minorities in Canada. I hope that we pass the Bill and that we pass it quickly. I would ask those provinces out there in the country that also deal with language minority groups, whether the English language minority in Quebec or the Francophone minorities in Ontario, in the Atlantic Provinces and in the west, to do likewise as we are doing here today in this House, namely, to follow the example of this Parliament, this Government and the previous Government and protect the minority language groups in Canada as they should be protected and as the Constitution of Canada has pointed the way.

Madam Speaker, I was very interested, as I always am, in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Ailmand). He certainly talked a lot about Meech Lake. I think he said more about Meech Lake here this afternoon on Bill C-72 than perhaps he did when the Accord was being debated initially. I will not come to that for the moment.
His closing remarks were on Bill 101, which I am glad the Member mentioned because he comes from the province where that Bill has caused so much political discontent and/or, frankly, betrayal, as I read the papers. In view of what was said in election campaigns and what has actually been done, with the Hon. Member, coming from that province where Bill 101 does adversely affect a good bulk of Canadians within that province, would he be prepared to have conversations with his House Leader on this House doing what we did on the Manitoba language question of passing a resolution asking the Quebec Government to move on Bill 101 and/or to fulfil its promises made in the election campaign? Or will we just sit back and wait until the Supreme Court perhaps comes down and helps resolve the problem?

Madam Speaker, if the Government House Leader were to make such a proposal, I would certainly approach my House Leader and ask for support of such a resolution, similar to the one in the case of Manitoba. By all means, I encourage the Government to come forward with such a resolution. We will be glad to discuss it on this side.
I agree with the Hon. Member that fairness must be done on all sides. The same fairness that we are attempting to provide at the federal level must also apply in provinces. That is why I
Official Languages Act
said I hoped Ontario one day will opt in totally to the constitutional provisions in the Constitution Act of 1982. That is why I ask Quebec to follow the example that we are setting here.
We passed the Meech Lake Accord. Let Quebec respond in like kind and pass legislation that would take away those repressive parts of Bill 101.
By the way, I must inform my hon. friend that I spoke at great length on the Meech Lake Accord when it was before the House.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Ailmand). He said the distinct society clause is simply to protect the French fact in Quebec. We have not yet had an interpretation by the courts of the meaning of the phrase distinct society. Is the Member not afraid that once we get a ruling from the Supreme Court of Canada, distinct society might mean all sorts of things, similar to what we have seen lately concerning the abortion legislation which has been struck down by the Supreme Court of Canada. Nobody knew about it, but it happened. We are leaving a lot to be desired because the court might interpret that distinct clause differently than the Member does, then Bill 101 might stay forever.

Madam Speaker, perhaps I was speaking too quickly but I certainly did not define distinct society in the way in which the Hon. Member just quoted me.
I said that the distinct society was not defined in the Meech Lake Accord and consequently I did not know how others could interpret it to mean that it would eliminate minority language rights in Canada or in Quebec. That is what I said. I went on to point out that since the distinct society has no definition in the Meech Lake Accord, it is not defined, it cannot be interpreted to come into contradiction with other parts of the Meech Lake Accord which are clear. What is clear is what is called the duality clause. It says that a fundamental characteristic of Canada is that we have French language minority groups outside of Quebec, that we have an English language group inside Quebec and that the Governments of Canada and the provinces must preserve those minority groups. That is very clear in the Meech Lake Accord. The distinct society clause is not defined.

Madam Speaker, 1 understood what the Hon. Member said but I wonder, when he voted in favour of Meech Lake, he voted for something that was not defined. I think it is dangerous for the House to let the courts decide the definition of a distinct society. It might override Bill C-72. The courts might say that because of the distinct society clause, the Bill is going to apply only in English Canada and will not apply in Quebec because Quebec has to preserve its own language.

February 8, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The constitutional amendment overrides any legislation by Parliament, as we have seen lately with respect to the abortion issue. Does the Hon. Member agree with me on that?

No, Madam Speaker, as a lawyer, in my wildest imaginings, 1 do not know how nine judges of the Supreme Court could interpret the distinct character clause in that way when in the very next paragraph it says that the Parliament and Governments of Canada must preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada and I put accent on "fundamental" characteristic of Canada which is that there is an English-speaking community in Quebec which must be preserved and French-speaking groups in the other provinces which must be preserved. That is a fundamental characteristic of Canada. How nine judges collectively in a majority decision could just ignore that clause and interpret the distinct society clause to do away with all English-speaking rights, as a lawyer 1 cannot see that. Some people are arguing that way but they are completely ignoring the duality clause which is only one sentence away from the distinct society clause. They are completely ignoring that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as Member for Madawaska-Victoria in New Brunswick, as an Acadian and a Francophone outside Quebec, I am honoured and privileged to join in this important debate on Bill C-72 respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada.
I would be remiss if, from the outset, I failed to underscore the historic character of the legislation now under consideration. We all know that this Bill is the first major reform of the Official Languages Act since it was adopted in 1969, yet however valid and avant-garde it may have been at the time no one would question the urgent need for reconsidering and redrafting the law to reflect Canada's changing requirements and new circumstances.
The legislation had to be adapted to the new constitutional and political realities of this country so that it would be a more satisfactory reflection of the linguistic changes that have taken place in Canadian society. Needless to say, Madam Speaker, Bill C-72 goes well beyond these two prerequisites, covering all major aspects of the language question. Today, however, I would prefer to highlight some aspects of the Bill that are particularly important to me as an Acadian and a Francophone from a region outside Quebec. 1 am thinking more specifically of the Government's new responsibility for promoting and developing official language communities and the special place this Bill has in the process of promoting and implementing the French fact in Canada.
I said that this Bill was drafted in order to provide urgently needed legislation. Actually, it was necessary to update the Official Languages Act, 1969, to bring it into line with the constitutional requirements of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In this respect, there are some important provisions regarding the language of work in the federal Public Service, service to the public across this country, full participation by French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians in federal institutions, and the administration of justice. Furthermore, as I said earlier, it was necessary to adapt our official languages legislation to the linguistic changes in Canadian society. In fact, tremendous progress has been made in this respect since 1969. Hence the need for a better definition of the roles and responsibilities of the various departments responsible for implementing the new policy, and also the need for determining the parameters of federal-provincial cooperation involving the enhancement of official language communities and, finally, the need for expanding opportunities for learning the other official language.

1 truly believe that Bill C-72 reaches all of its initial objectives. In fact, the introduction of Bill C-72 in the House on June 25, 1987, was greeted throughout the country by a wave of approval by the opposition Parties, the Commissioner of Official Languages, and representatives of the Anglophone communities in Quebec and the Francophone communities outside of Quebec unanimously agreed on the value and depth of the proposed changes.

The Constitutional Accord signed by all First Ministers on June 3 recognized, as was mentioned earlier by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East
February 8, 1988

(Mr. Allmand), that the existence of French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians in all regions of the country constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada, a characteristic that Parliament and all provincial legislatures now have a duty to protect thanks to this Accord, and this should, in my opinion, be considered a substantial step forward in the age old struggle waged by Francophones for recognition of their language rights.
As I pointed out in this Flouse on October 1 of last year, representatives of French-speaking groups outside Quebec and supporters of their cause would have liked all governments to be given the role of promoting as well as preserving the fundamental characteristic recognized in this Accord. But we know, as all Honourable Members do, that in spite of the efforts of the Prime Minister of Canada himself, his provincial counterparts could not agree on such an objective. This noncommitment on the part of provincial partners, which I hope is circumstantial and temporary, should not prevent us from proceeding resolutely in that direction with regard to matters and in areas under our jurisdiction. So I am glad to read in the preamble of this legislation that the Canadian government is committed, and I quote:
-to enhancing the vitality and supporting the development of English and French linguistic minority communities, as an integral part of the two official language communities of Canada, and to fostering full recognition and use of English and French in Canadian society;
Moreover, this legislation reflects our government's commitment, and I quote:
-to cooperating with provincial governments and their institutions to support the development of English and French linguistic minority communities, to provide services in both English and French, to respect the constitutional guarantees of minority language educational rights and to enhance opportunities for all to learn both English and French;

It should be understood that the official languages policy of Canada was not intended to force all Canadians to become bilingual. That is important. On the contrary, the policy allows for the majority of Francophones and Anglophones of our country to function on a day-to-day basis in their first official language, and even to remain unilingual if they so desire. However, this policy does require federal authorities, and encourages the provinces and the private sector, to become bilingual with a view to bridging the gap between citizens and communities of both French and English backgrounds.
My own riding of Madawaska-Victoria is 75 per cent Francophone and 25 per cent Anglophone. Unless the public authorities there can serve these communities in their own official languages, there will be chaos, and this is what we are attempting to do.
[ Translation]
And as my colleague, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations and Leader of the Government in the Senate, senator Lowell Murray, was saying quite appropriately in Quebec City on June 26 of last year, and I quote:
Official Languages Act
Bridges can only be useful if we prevent both banks they link together from
crumbling.
Madam Speaker, that is why 1 consider that in promoting and supporting linguistic communities, a role the government assumes under Bill C-72, we are dealing with one of the most important and essential aspects of our new language policy.
According to that logic, indeed, could we on the one hand force the federal Government to offer its services in both official languages everywhere in the country and, on the other hand, abandon linguistic communities to their fate without protecting them nor promoting their development?
I am also happy the Secretary of State has been given the responsibility of inciting, encouraging and co-ordinating the fulfilment within other federal institutions of that commitment to help official languages communities prosper and develop.
Allow me, Madam Speaker, to point out that the Department of the Secretary of State did not wait for the coming into force of the new Act to show it was interested in honouring that commitment. The national program that was launched last September to create community radio stations for official languages communities is a very good example of the new role the Department of the Secretary of State, and hence the Government, will be able to play in the social, economic and cultural development of those communities.
I hope that program, as other similar measures, will help the representatives of those communities understand that, contrary to what some of them may say, they are not the great losers in the 1987 Constitutional Accord.
Other departments such as Employment and Immigration also prove to be much more open towards the development of our linguistic communities. For instance, this very day and more exactly one hour ago, in Edmonton, in the province of Alberta, the Department of Employment and Immigration signed a contract worth over $40,000 for personnel replacement and community development training, for a group of nine anglophone organizations in Alberta.
I think we will see other similar initiatives come from this new legislation, and the whole country will benefit.
Madam Speaker, allow me to expand for a moment on the importance of this language policy for the affirmation of the French fact in Canada. The tabling of Bill C-72 is not an isolated and inconsequent move. As I already said, it is part of the whole evolution of the Canadian society, and the result or end-product of more than 20 years of reflection and analysis about official languages.
Consequently, it is not, in its form and content, foreign to the values and concepts put forward by the Canadian Government during 20 years of language policy.
However, when we look at the path followed by our Government, this Bill takes a particular significance. It is consistent with our objectives respecting national reconciliation, social justice and international influence.

February 8, 1988
Official Languages Act
On the international scene in particular Canada, thanks to its dual identity, is able to enjoy with French-speaking countries, within the Francophonie, newly created at the second summit held in Quebec, the same kind of special relationship it has enjoyed with English-speaking countries within the Commonwealth.
The second summit of countries which have French as a common language, held in Quebec in September, and later the Commonwealth summit, in Vancouver, strengthened the international stature of Canada. It would be ironic on our part to try and play a major role within these two international organizations while neglecting, at home, these two languages and the communities which use them.
Madam Speaker, our official languages communities shall not be left alone in their undertaking towards the preservation and promotion of their culture and heritage. Because their heritage is also ours!
Madam Speaker, I was particularly pleased with the positive and serene atmosphere in which this Bill has been prepared, presented and received. This feeling is all the more vividly felt for me since I had the opportunity of following very closely the painful debate which took place in New Brunswick in 1984 and 1985, during the review process of the province's Official Languages Act.
Indeed, Acadians and the French speaking community had been anxiously awaiting since 1980 for their provincial Government to re-examine in its turn the language legislation passed as well by the New Brunswick legislature in 1969.
I take opportunity of this debate, Madam Speaker, as did my colleague the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace- Lachine-East (Mr. Allmand), to call once more upon New Brunswick political leaders. I strongly urge them to enact the positions they have sustained in the past and to adopt as soon as possible, following the example of the federal Government, a clearer, more articulate, more open and more generous linguistic law, a law that would have a wider scope and, finally, that would better represent the social fabric of the province.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I wish perhaps to underline the leading and exemplary role the Prime Minister has played in order to bring about this linguistic reform. For us it would have been difficult-perhaps even impossible-to undertake such an initiative if we could not have relied on people like the Prime Minister who was able to give us a coherent and articulate insight into what Canada is today and what it should be tomorrow. I sincerely commend him for his unwavering will to work towards erecting a Canadian society based on justice, tolerance, fairness and respect.
I also want to congratulate my colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the Secretary of State, the former President of the Treasury Board-and the new President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) who is continuing the
work-for producing a well-balanced, responsible and, in many respects, avant-garde measure. Members of the Senate and House of Commons committee-and I see my colleague the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) is here-did not spare any effort with respect to this Bill and they deserve our congratulations.
Madam Speaker, my closing remarks are directed to my colleagues in the House. 1 urge them to give generous support to this Bill and promote it in their respective ridings. This morning I heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) say that as Members we should all go to our ridings and promote this Bill on the official languages. I agree with her and I hope that all Members of the House will support this Bill and promote it in their respective regions.
Madam Speaker, I am convinced that Bill C-72 will mark the long awaited new beginning in the realm of the official languages, and I think we all have every reason to be proud.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question to the Hon. Member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Val-court) about the Province of Quebec, which is adjacent to his own province.
What is his position on Quebec Bill 101 and on the protection of the English language in that province? Would he support a resolution of this House asking Quebec to withdraw Bill 101?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, earlier today during the Oral Question Period, I told a Member who had asked me a question about the economic development policy of British Columbia that, in my personal opinion, it would go against our national reconciliation policy to interfere in areas under provincial jurisdiction.
Bill 101 is an issue which obviously concerns the Quebec Government, and it is also taking a new dimension with the Meech Lake Accord. Once implemented, the constitutional amendments contained in the Accord guarantee to Quebec and English-speaking Quebecers not only their survival, but also their promotion within Quebec. 1 am certain that the Quebec Government will adapt its own laws to the new circumstances when the Meech Lake Accord is approved, as I hope it will be, by every province in Canada.

Madam Speaker, 1 have a couple of questions. With regard to the question of my hon. friend from Calgary East (Mr. Kindy), I understand why Parliament does not often trespass on provincial jurisdiction. However, the fact is that this Parliament, under a former regime, had a history of passing resolutions when provincial history was being changed by language law.
February 8, 1988

The first such resolution came before this Chamber on October 6, 1983. In 1983 the Parliament of Canada in effect passed a directive to the Manitoba Legislature on its language question. We could do the same thing with regard to Bill 101. The next time the issue came up was on February 24, 1984, with "whereases" which could be changed slightly to tell the Province of Quebec that it is abrogating history with regard to Bill 101. However, we will leave Bill 101 aside.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) spoke this morning but our rules do not allow us to ask the Minister questions. I would therefore like to ask this Minister a couple of short questions and, depending upon his answer, perhaps a brief supplementary question.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development); Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I take exception to the Member referring to Members who ask questions about this
Bill. This Bill is before the House for debate and we should let all Members pose questions. The questions that have been asked deserve consideration and it is the right, indeed the obligation, of Members of the House to address this Bill seriously and air those concerns. They have been elected to come and represent the interests of their constituents. I take exception to the Member's statement.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter the debate on Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada. This legislation needs serious reflection because it is the kind of legislation that must have the benefit of knowledge and facts rather than emotion and exaggerated statements. Our comments on this legislation must reflect our concern for unity and harmony in this country and for a consensus with regard to official languages.
During my remarks I want to deal with the question of official languages, the kind of debate with which we are involved today, as well as to deal with some very serious shortcomings in the legislation.
Until now, the official languages legislation was the product of the Liberal Party. Today is an historical occasion because the introduction of this new legislation by the Conservative Party means that the issue of official languages has moved from being a partisan subject to being a non- partisan issue. The policy of official bilingualism has been supported from the outset by the New Democratic Party.
Bilingualism has a negative meaning to many people. To some, in the worst parlance, it means that French is being shoved down their throats, that they must learn another language and cannot work in the federal Public Service unless they are bilingual. Of course, that is a distortion of the reality because bilingualism means that Canadians can speak their own language without having to learn the other. It means that English-speaking western Canadians do not have to learn French, because Canadians can live in their own language.
Of course, we hope that that right will only encourage Canadians to choose to learn the other official language or any of the other languages that are spoken in this country.
Clearly, once people understand that they have this right to live in their community and speak their mother tongue, they will feel secure enough to enjoy the benefits from learning the other languages that exist in this country.
We must understand that the official language policy means that Canadians have the right to live and work in their own language without having to learn the other.
The official languages Bill is an historic development because it means the end to social prejudice which gave rise to comments such as "speak white" to French Canadians and gave rise to an attitude that somehow French Canadians were less than equal to English-speaking Canadians. It means an end to prejudice and discrimination which led to some powerful and articulate poetry based on those attitudes.
February 8, 1988

This legislation is a first step toward equality and we must approach it with some understanding as to the meaning of bilingualism while setting aside some of the distortions that have been propagated over the years.
Let us consider the debate in which we are engaged with regard to the Official Languages Act. I suggest it is essential that it be a non-partisan debate that is characterized by its capacity to educate and shed light on this subject, not from an adversarial or political point of view, but on the basis of understanding. It is only through understanding the legislation and through understanding the different communities in our country that we will be able to preserve the unity of Canada. Only in this way will we be able to continue to have a country called Canada.
The debate must be democratic and open. We must listen to all sides of the issue. We must listen to those who are strong proponents of the legislation, those who indicate the need for such legislation. At the same time we must be open to those who have concerns about the legislation, people who say that aspects of it go too far. It is only when people can speak up about the legislation without fear that we can have a useful and open debate and that language policy will find an acceptable place in Canada.
I want to point out one thing about the debate, not only in the House but in the country, with respect to what it should not be. I refer specifically now to a magazine called the Western Report. On the front cover of a recent issue it stated: "Si vous ne pouvez pas lire ceci, vous ne pouvez pas travaiUer pour le gouvernement federal." It then states: "Translation: If you can't read this, you can't work for the federal Government." I just sat here to read the legislation. What this says is a complete and utter distortion of the reality of the legislation. It is a complete and utter distortion of the official languages policy of Canada. This so-called contribution to the debate is what subtracts from it rather than adds to it. This type of characterization of the legislation with which we are dealing is unfortunate. It adds nothing to the debate. In fact, it makes it much more difficult.
Rather than respond to those types of distortions which particular writers place on the legislation, let us remind ourselves that, while this legislation recognizes that there are two official languages in Canada, both French and English enjoy an equal status. The legislation also has its limits. It should have limits. No legislation should be without limits.
Let me point out specifically what I mean when I say that this legislation should have limits. With respect to the right to work concerning those in the federal service, officers and employees of all federal institutions would have the right to use either official language. That is a pretty broad and sweeping principle. I happen to think it is a good one. However, I point
Official Languages Act
out that the principle is limited in its application, as I think it should be. That is reasonable.
This part of the legislation is limited to head offices of federal institutions. It is limited to federal institutions in the National Capital Region. It is limited to federal institutions in other prescribed regions. It does not apply in an unlimited fashion. It is necessary to make these points in order to bring reason back into the debate and to put aside the distortions that lead to excessive emotion with regard to this subject.
With respect to the provisions concerning service, we need provisions with regard to service in the official languages of our country. People must be assured that they can receive service in their own official language. However, those provisions are limited, as I think they should be. They are limited with regard to service to those areas where there is a significant demand for the service. It does not apply to every place and all over but to places where there is a significant demand.
Let us bring some rationality and some reason back to the debate so that we can progress with regard to unity. This will enable us to amend such legislation when it is indicated that an amendment is appropriate. It does not have to be all or nothing. One should not be accused of being a racist if one raises questions about such legislation. One should not be accused of giving special privileges to one group if one is in favour of this legislation. We must bring reason to the debate. We need to stay away from excessive emotion and partisanship. The debate must be open to all sides of the issue.
I now wish to make a couple of points about the legislation which are critical. This legislation deserves to be criticized because it is important legislation. It falls short in two respects. 1 refer to the provisions affecting the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. With regard to the Yukon, the Yukon is treated as a federal institution in this legislation, while the Northwest Territories is exempted from such designation. Why not exempt the Yukon from the provision as well? Why not respect the legislative authority of the Yukon? In that respect this legislation is ham-fisted. It is too heavy. It ought to show some respect for the local authorities.
With respect to the Northwest Territories, it has an Official Languages Act. Yet there are provisions in this Bill which state that in order for the Northwest Territories legislation to be amended it would require the concurrence of the Parliament of Canada. Surely, that provision should not be there. The legislative authority of the Northwest Territories should be respected. We live in a country which has a federal system of government. That means that we respect the jurisdictions of different legislatures. In that respect this legislation falls short. It must be amended.
I have heard from some quarters of the House concerns with regard to the provisions affecting courts. Those provisions need to be examined critically. Surely, we need a court system

February 8, 1988
Social Insurance Numbers
which is capable of serving people in their own language. However, that does not mean that every judge in every court in the country has to speak both official languages. We need to approach this debate in an open fashion, a fashion that will allow, permit and enhance the unity of our country. We must approach the debate about official languages from the perspective of what we have in common as Canadians.
We have one common citizenship. We are all Canadians. There is but one Canada. It is only when we start from that premise that we can then move forward to celebrate and recognize the differences that we have. They are differences in language and culture. They provide a strong foundation upon which to build our official languages policy.

He said: Madam Speaker, anyone who is watching this debate could assume that the process was a democratic one, that elected representatives of the people would debate the merits of this Bill and vote according to choice. The reality is different. The process is a triumph of bureaucracy not democracy. It is a charade of Parliament. We will debate the merits of the Bill but the decision has already been made. The elected representatives of the people will not have a chance to vote at all. That has already been decided. There will be enough speakers to maintain the debate until 6 p.m. when the Speaker will assume that a motion to adjourn the House has been made.
This debate has usually been called "talking out". It is very familiar, and because of its familiarity it has gained a certain legitimacy. It is unworthy of Parliament. I have to believe that it is a form of legislative "coitus interrupts" which is the term for the ancient Roman method of birth control that prevented conception simply by bringing the whole process to an end when a decision could be made. So here we are, the House witnessing the possibility of legislative life being snuffed out by
interfering with the process. We are here to talk not to vote, that is the message.
I have to ask, why would this Bill suffer such a fate? Not for the obvious reason that one Minister or many Ministers do not want it to become a law. We know that, because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the Minister responsible for the law affecting the social insurance numbers, spoke in favour of such a Bill when he was a Private Member. We remember when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) as a Private Member introduced a Bill comparable to Bill C-236. He cannot be against it. Well, who is? Who wants to talk it out? It is not the elected Government. It is the appointed Government. So such is my inference, that Canada, as I have observed in the years that I have served in the House, has two Governments. There is an elected Government that is accountable to the people; and there is a Government by appointed officials, accountable mainly to each other. Their hand reaches out everywhere in this capital, including the precincts of Parliament. Some are eminent, such as Deputy Ministers and senior officials. Others are not, such as ministerial assistants. But all have power, including the power to shape what will happen on the floor of the House of Commons, a House they cannot enter, but which they can affect.
The result today is that we will have a masquerade ball in which Members of the House will dance a parliamentary minuet with one another, according to music that the bureaucrats have chosen. I understand why bureaucrats would make such a decision, for this is the type of Bill that undercuts power. The assumption of all bureaucracy is that if there is anything they do not control, it is for one reason: they have chosen not to control it. This Bill is a threat to that. That is why, to use another figure of speech, it is going to be aborted.
In the information age knowledge is power. The more you know about a person, the more control you have over him or her. This is the reason that the very thought of reducing the opportunities of demanding the social insurance number of an individual is a threat to bureaucracy.
The social insurance number gives bureaucrats the chance to control us by giving them the key to start up the entire high-tech apparatus. Given the large number of government agencies and Departments, federal and provincial, now using the social insurance number, that number is the key to a mass of information about every one of us in this Chamber, everyone listening to this debate via television, everyone from coast to coast. Thus, the computer gives the bureaucrat an instrument of power such as none before him ever possessed.
When the social insurance number was first proposed, many Progressive Conservative Members of Parliament pointed out how it could become an instrument to identify each person in the country, a registration by which Governments could keep tabs on everyone. For example, the Right Hon. John Diefen-baker warned that it could become a national identifier that could be the basis for a national registration. When he heard that, Prime Minister Pearson insisted that it would never be so
February 8, 1988

used. When it was suggested that the social insurance number might be used for income tax as well as for unemployment insurance, he immediately interjected, "Certainly not".
The most startling feature of this entire travesty is the claim of Professor Flaherty, who has made an exhaustive study of the social insurance number, and who stated: "The House of Commons was never asked in 1964, or at any other time, to authorize or ratify the introduction of social insurance numbers, which was essentially a decision of the Unemployment Insurance Commission". There you have it, Mr. Speaker, from the very conception, through the delivery, through the growth, it has been fathered, mothered, nurtured, educated and bred by bureaucracy.
Since then it has become the legislated right of 19 federal agencies to require that individuals report their number when seeking service. And they are not all. Without legislation, other agencies have began demanding it, as have provincial Governments, and hospitals. By abusing the social insurance number it has become possible to gain a great, illicit, unmerited grasp of a person's life including many dimensions of his or her life that should be private. One can learn what is the hospital history of a person, whether she has had an abortion, whether he has been admitted to a psychiatric centre. Now such is the abuse of this by Governments.
I want to point out briefly that the potential abuse of the social insurance number is not confined to Governments, for bureaucracy is not confined to Governments. Bureaucracy is a state of mind, and it is found in the corporate dimension of the private sector. The private sector does not as a whole abhor bureaucracy. The entrepreneurs do, and the small business people do. They want to live and work as free individuals and serve other free individuals.
But people who are at home in the mass of corporate structures of the private sector have the same mentality as those who are at home in the massive organizational structure of governments. What difference is there between the management of a government Department and the management of a corporation department? Not very much. Neither assumes that the shareholders own it. They act, whether in government or in corporation, as though management owned it. That is why so many government officials can readily move into corporations and then come back to government. One can almost describe a certain two-way traffic between Toronto and Ottawa in certain dimensions of government. A person may come out of university, come to Ottawa and learn all about a Department, then go down to Toronto or perhaps to Montreal and be in business. They know all the loopholes, how to exploit them, and then they return to Ottawa as a senior official and rewrite the law. One environment is the same as the other. Each is an environment of bureaucracy, and each has the same passion for control of people.
We often find that elements in the private sector are as eager to abuse this as elements in the public sector. The social insurance number is now demanded of customers and
Social Insurance Numbers
employees as though a corporation had a right to it. A person opening a bank account may have to report it. A person applying for a job may have to report it. A person wanting insurance may have to report it. One may ask: Why not? What is wrong with that? This is what is wrong with it: the accumulation of a vast continent of information, its reportability made possible by computers, means that anyone with the right key to this storehouse of data can learn about a person what should be that person's own.
The abuse of the social insurance number is thus an invasion of the privacy to which every citizen in a democracy is entitled. We ought to see the threat that is before each of us. The social insurance number is a key which can open the door to a person's life revealing that which is his own.
Here is a man complaining that two large food chains in Newfoundland demand the social insurance number before cashing cheques. Here is an Ottawa woman reporting that a local hospital emergency ward demanded that her number be reported before she could be admitted for medical treatment. Here is a New Brunswick man complaining that his union insisted its members give their numbers.
If Bill C-236 could only come to a vote, could take one more step toward becoming law, that could change. It would mean that no person, organization, group, or body could demand that a person disclose his social insurance number, and that no federal body should request it without setting out in writing what is the particular purpose for which it is needed and what Act of Parliament authorizes the disclosure. Any organization requesting the number would be required to advise the person that he or she is free to refuse it.
Our need for this legislation has been clear for years. On December 8, 1978, the then Hon. Member for Saskatoon- Biggar, the Minister of Justice gave a carefully crafted, vigorously worded plea for a similar Bill to Bill C-236. He said:
My real worry arises from the real possibility that use of a single identifying number, such as SIN, in more and more computer files makes it easier and cheaper for organizations to exchange data among themselves and to merge records from files of different agencies, departments and organizations into central data banks. There arises the ultimate possibility that a person with access to the data banks will be able to compile a complete dossier on any individual.
1 recognize that some people, perhaps some Hon. Members, may wonder whether that is a critical threat to a person with nothing dishonest, nothing illegal, or nothing subversive to hide. The threat is real. The more a government knows about us, the more power it has over us. The more corporate data manipulators know about us, the more they can exploit us. This is why the Government of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) planned legislation to restrict the use of the social insurance number. The defeat of that Government meant that that legislation did not see the light of day until the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe, the

February 8, 1988
Social Insurance Numbers
Minister of National Defence, introduced a Private Member's Bill in 1980, as did Senator Jacques Flynn in the other place. Other Bills have been introduced over the years by the Flon. Member for Saskatoon-Biggar, the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen), and Mr. John Gamble when he was a Member of the House. In March, 1987 the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General reported that it shared the concerns expressed in these initiatives and recommended changes to the Privacy Act that would achieve many of the objectives of Bill C-236.
When we face this kind of threat to our privacy and hence to our freedom; when we see this issue excite the concern of Hon. Members over many years, patiently returning to the House when one Bill after another has been talked out according to the process that I have described; and when we see a government wanting to take initiative to bring in some control over the use and abuse of the social insurance number, I must ask: Why should we wait any longer? Here is a Bill to be voted on and if approved by the House to be sent to committee. We are not allowed to use the word "hypocrisy", but if we were, we would certainly think of it if we were to describe the process which says that we cannot accept the Bill because it has something wrong with it. What human composition ever lacks something wrong with it? Any Bill which comes into the House invites amendment and improvement. This is what committees are for. If some part of a Bill is deficient and needs to be corrected, the committee is the place to do it. This debate is to focus on the principle of the legislation, and if we are satisfied as a House, then we can work on the refinement of the Bill itself.
Why wait? Why not today strike a blow for liberty by restoring some of every Canadian's privacy? I ask that question but I know the answer, for since there will not be a vote on the Bill we cannot strike a blow for liberty. Liberty has struck out.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the Hon. Member who just made a very eloquent and compassionate speech to the House. I paid very close attention to his remarks, and I cannot think of anything but praise for the Hon. Member on his effort today in not only convincing Members of the House of the necessity of such legislation but in indeed trying to convince anyone who cares to listen that some people who are not elected unfortunately wield much power around this place and in other circles of government. That message which he gave to us is as important as the Bill which he proposed to the House. Again I reiterate my sincere congratulations.
The issue which the Hon. Member brings to our attention is certainly not a new one. Indeed, from its very inception Members of the House have been concerned with possible misuse of social insurance numbers. The authors of the initiative never contemplated that social insurance numbers
would be used, and I would add abused, the way that they are today.
In his annual report of 1986-87, which was tabled in the House, the Privacy Commissioner described some of the worst cases of misuse of social insurance numbers. Let me read a few of them. The first one reads:
The Privacy Commissioner's participation on CBC's Cross Country Checkup generated an entire two hours of calls about the use and abuse of SIN. One caller, a woman from the Maritimes, told the Commissioner that unemployed workers were required to put their SIN on the outside of the envelope in which they send employment reports to EIC.
The Commissioner, concerned about her allegations, inquired about the practice. In fact, the offending envelope had been replaced some time earlier with one that does not ask for SINs. The regional office has been using up its large stock.
In other words, what we had was a government agency not only requiring social insurance numbers to be used but asking that they actually be displayed within public view on the outside of envelopes. Here is another example which concerns all of us:
Another caller was upset because Canada Post insisted on a SIN before releasing registered mail. The postal clerk had rejected three other pieces of identification, insisting on the SIN. The clerk relented only when the woman asked that the letter be returned to sender.
How many people would take that amount of time and trouble in order to refuse the giving up of private information such as is the social insurance number? Most people just give in and say, "I don't have time for this argument," provide the social insurance number, as wrong as that is, and go on doing their daily business.
The now Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) in
1978	and the now Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in
1979	both proposed in this House a reform of the use of social insurance numbers. Today, of course, those two Members of Parliament are cabinet Ministers. 1 know that they are listening attentively to the remarks that I am making today and they will want to convey to the rest of their cabinet colleagues my comments and even, more important, the comments of the Hon. Member who proposed the Bill to us. It is my hope that if the Government talks this Bill out today, which I know is the fear of the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) because he took great pains to express that to us, at least on the second day of debate the Government will have had time to reconsider doing that. Perhaps there is a message out there to all Canadians to lobby their Members of Parliament whoever they are, whatever Party or constituency they represent, including cabinet Ministers, to ensure that this Bill or one like it is passed by this Parliament.
There are, of course-and the Government will take great pains in telling us that-flaws in the Bill. A number of government bills have flaws in them. We were discussing a government initiative earlier today known as the conflict of interest code. A few people found things wrong with that
February 8, 1988

particular initiative. It was a government initiative proposed in this House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
There are several other initiatives-I am only using that as an example-of government legislation, which are flawed. Many Bills are introduced in this House and when they are presented to us, they are often, at second reading, filled with amendments. In committee we sometimes get amendments that are so broad that legislation has to be withdrawn and reintroduced. The fact that there may be failures in this Bill, and if there are any failures they are not major, is not an excuse for anyone to refuse having this Bill to come to a vote.
My wish would be that the Bill would have primacy over other legislation to ensure that no other government agency passes or causes an Act to be passed by this Parliament or any other so that we can prevent the use of social insurance numbers by other government Departments. That is not quite covered in the Bill. We could tighten up that provision at committee. Notwithstanding that, what is in the Bill is far better than what is there now because what is there now is almost nothing at all.

I would like to take a few moments to share with you, Madam Speaker and Hon. Members, some of my personal experience with the use of unemployment insurance numbers.
A few years ago, when I was a Member of the Ontario Legislature, I received a phone call at my parliamentary office in Toronto. My wife was calling to let me know that Julie, our little girl who had just started nursery school, was given an envelope that morning she was asked to take home to her parents. So Julie had put the envelope in her school bag and brought it home. The envelope was from the school and contained a form to apply for a social insurance number. This was for a four-year-old child!
I was very upset. 1 called the school and 1 asked them: What on earth are you sending us this for? Why did you ask our daughter to take this envelope home and give it to her parents to complete and send back to the school? School authorities simply said: Well, that is the policy of the school board. Here, a number is given to each child on the first day of school. So the policy of the school board was then to give each four-year old a social insurance number. Why, Madam Speaker? I have no idea. I was never given a reason.
You can be sure that the next day 1 rose in the Legislative Assembly to ask the then Minister of Education, Mrs. Bette Stephenson, why school boards asked for the children's social insurance numbers. She replied: That is nonsense, of course, no school board has such a requirement. I rose and presented her with the envelope my daughter Julie had been given the day before.
Needless to say the Minister was startled and that a few days later the school board made it known it no longer insisted children needed a social insurance number.
Social Insurance Numbers
Our daughter who is now 10 years old still does not have a social insurance number, and I wonder why she would need one at that age. You would be astonished to learn how often she was asked for one to participate in a sport or other activities, as if it was thoroughly acceptable for a child to have his or her social insurance number. I still ask myself the same question: why?

Orwell in his book, 1984, was predicting that governments would have big computers, the big brother of government as he referred to it, that would have massive amounts of data on people. In a way, he was carrying it a bit far but in another way he was still, nevertheless, close to the point. However, it is not as much big government that has made most of the abuse, it is big government that has permitted others to abuse the system even more than governments have done it themselves, to such a point that I have even entered buildings and have been asked to register and indicate my social insurance number.
Those practices are totally unacceptable, and I think all Members of this House would agree that they are. It was not a federal government building but it was a form of government building, to answer my friend from Winnipeg. There is indeed a need for legislation as proposed to us by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West.
I am sure that if all Members took the time to inform themselves of the abuses of this system and the potential abuses in the future, not just by governments but by corporations that can exchange data of all sorts merely with a social insurance number which, as we know, is not kept privately enough, then that misuse is cause for concern.
Let me conclude by reading an article written by Vicki Barnett of The Calgary Herald on July 14, 1987. She said:
The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce asked for it when I opened an account there. I needed to give it for family allowance. Years ago, I couldn't get a student loan without it, and when I studied journalism at Toronto's Ryerson Polytechnical Institute, my SIN was my student identification number. Credit agencies use it to keep track of my credit record. Some retailers want it as identification on cheques, and there is even a local 7-11 video club that demands it before you can obtain a membership.
Clearly, Madam Speaker, Orwell was not too far off.

February 8, 1988
Social Insurance Numbers
legislation which should go to committee to be studied, if those Hon. Members were named publicly, it would put a little pressure on them and perhaps persuade them to give this legislation the serious consideration it deserves.
1 believe this legislation ought to go to committee. The subject ought to be studied. We have to take seriously the concerns expressed by Canadians about the use of social insurance numbers. I have been spending considerable time visiting my constituents and this is one of the things that was brought up frequently. One gentleman who lives in my riding of Winnipeg North Centre is doing quite a study on the use of the SIN number. He has documents from the Privacy Commissioner. He points out the limitations of any citizen who tries to assert his or her right not to divulge his SIN number if he does not wish. He finds that this is a right which is honoured more in the breach than in the practice.
We have to study the way in which the social insurance number is used. On the basis of fact and understanding we have to come to some appreciation of what the number is used for and when its use turns into abuse. There is something to be balanced here. The balance is between privacy and the capacity to get things done. We have a social insurance number because of the need for organization. Yet if the number is used appropriately, I am sure people would accept its existence. However, if it is abused, then serious questions are raised. Therefore, we must examine how the number is being used and abused these days.
I do not know whether Hon. Members recall when the social insurance number was introduced or for what purpose. I am sure it was introduced for some specific and limited purpose. For the life of me, I could not really say exactly what. I am sure it has something to do with the administration of federal social programs. But that is the dilemma we find ourselves in. We know it was introduced some time ago for a good reason and it grew like Topsy. Now it is popping up all over the place. In an age of large organizations and instant communication, the age of the computer, this information on Canadian citizens can be collected very easily. It is time to examine how the social insurance number is used and to what extent it is being abused. It is time to recognize that the social insurance number is just the tip of the iceberg in a modern information age in which we once again must define and assert the notion of privacy. Our individual privacy has to do with our own individual power to assert ourselves as individual citizens rather than being abused by those who can surreptiously collect information about us in ways which were never intended.
I do not want to talk this Bill out. I want the Bill to go to committee which will result in a thorough and public study of the use and abuse of the social insurance number. It is time we did this.
