Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure this afternoon to speak in support of Bill C-236 which was introduced by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). This is not the first time a Bill such as this has been brought before the House, nor would I expect it to be the last. It is rather unfortunate that apparently this Bill has not been selected for the five hours of debate and then a vote. Far be it for me to make any critical comments about the committee of my colleagues which makes the selection. However, I would hope that if this Bill does return to the Order Paper at some time in the future, such a selection will be made. I think it deserves much more than one short hour's debate. It is something that should be voted upon.
I am speaking in support of this Bill but I cannot be as forceful, as eloquent or as knowledgeable as the Hon. Member who presented the Bill. I think there is a tendency for Members to become somewhat repetitive due to the fact that when one decides to speak on an issue and starts making notes, it seems that everyone has the same things in mind. Everyone is worried about social insurance numbers starting off with a very limited use and then being used more and more until abuse is built into the system with much more potential for abuse, so that we must look at ways in which this might be controlled. Forgive me, Madam Speaker, if I repeat a few of the points made beforehand.
We have to look with good intent at the spread which has taken place. It has been insidious but it has not been done deliberately and maliciously.
Social insurance numbers were originally brought in with a good purpose in mind. We needed an indentifier for social programs such as unemployment insurance and the Canada Pension Plan. There had to be some form of identification. But then it spread into the tax system because deductions for Canada Pension Plan and unemployment insurance were of interest to the tax Department and it was only natural that it would want to credit the right account. So it all made sense and it grew a little there.
Employers are required by law to deduct tax and unemployment insurance premiums and to remit that money to the Government. It is only logical, in a way, that they should require that same number so that the proper accounts could be credited. Because they have to use this number for every employee, it becomes natural for them to use that as an employee identification number. They could argue: "Why have two numbers? We have to use this one. Why not use it as our employee identification number?" So it grows bit by bit. The same applies to banks which sometimes are required to deduct tax payments on interest or at least provide someone with a T-5 form. It is the same thing with trust companies and stock brokers. They are required to credit dividend tax credits and so on. So it grows and grows and grows and so it spreads.
February 8, 1988

Perhaps the problem with the social insurance number is that it is just too useful. It is becoming a universal identifier for every reason. In the age of the computer, that can certainly lead to abuse. Everyone who has spoken on this has a vision in mind of what that abuse could be with the computers available to us today.
If this trend continues I can foresee the day when every baby born in Canada will be held upside down and have a social insurance number tattooed on the sole of his or her foot. Then, later on in life, someone will punch a button on a computer and up will come the history of that child from birth. All the taxes paid and taxes owing; where the person lived and lives; marital history and what they were up to when they were not married; how much they owe in maintenance payments or anything else. There will be the child's medical records, list of assets and liabilities, criminal record if any, passports issued, and where that person has travelled around the world.
A veritable mine of information will be available at the push of a button. This information will be extremely useful to certain people and certain agencies. It will obviously be very useful to tax collectors. It will be useful to police investigating certain offences. It will be useful for people involved in assessing security risks and that type of thing.
As much as we do not like tax collectors, for example, we know they are necessary. The difficulty they, for example, may have in drawing the line is that if you have a useful tool, when do you not use that useful tool? That question has to be addressed. If that kind of a situation were to arise, would it be consistent with the relationship we expect in a free society between the state and its citizens? That is where we have to find the right balance.
In certain totalitarian states, and I believe the Soviet Union is an example, people are required to have with them all kinds of information to present on demand to the authorities. In South Africa people are required to have with them the so-called Book of Life which lists all manner of information about them. I know South Africans do not like having to carry around with them all that information to present to the authorities on demand. They consider it to be an abridgment of their freedom and their rights as citizens. They certainly resent the situation, and I would like to think that we are not coming to the same thing in Canada.
If this kind of information is available to Government, you can bet your bottom dollar it will also get into private hands. It is almost impossible to stop that from happening. Even if we have a degree of confidence in our Government, there are very few of us who would want that type of information to get into private hands as well.
How do we address these questions? Evidently a lot of thought has gone into the drafting of this Bill. I compliment
Social Insurance Numbers
the Member for that. He has presented some pretty good ideas which should be considered in detail with respect to the steps we must take to curb abuse or potential abuse. First he suggests the restriction of compulsory use of social insurance numbers to federal Government and agencies thereof. Provincial, municipal and private bodies would be unable to demand social insurance numbers. He proposes to make sure that any other persons who request a social insurance number must point out that it is not necessary that it be given. In addition, there can be no repercussions if the number is refused. He also creates a number of summary conviction offences and civil remedies if someone's rights have been abused.
Thank you very much indeed for giving me the opportunity to speak on this most important subject, Madam Speaker, and once again, I offer my congratulations to the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse).

Bill C-236 deals with a matter which is near and dear to many Canadians. The use of social insurance numbers has been ever-increasing since their introduction. Given the very important object of this Bill it is important that it be clearly understood. To foster this understanding it is necessary to look at the provisions of this Bill in some detail. This I propose to do. However, before I proceed, it is important that the issues which the Bill addresses are put into context. To do this, additional information is required.
First, in my view it would be helpful for Members to have the benefit of some information about the origin of the SIN and subsequent developments with respect to its use. It could also be useful to Members to be aware of a 1980 study which was done by the Privacy Commissioner concerning the extent to which the SIN was being used and the privacy implications arising from its uses.
I also believe it could be useful to Members to know more about the Privacy Act, which came into force on July 1, 1983, and how it affects the collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal of the social insurance number. Finally, it would be important to know what initiatives have been undertaken by the Government recently with regard to the social insurance number.
This information is important for two reasons. It will indicate why the social insurance number was created and how it is used. It will also help Members to identify the privacy implications which are associated with this number. Finally, and most important, it will permit Members to assess the controls proposed by the Bill in light of those which are currently in place and those which are now being undertaken by the Government.
The issues raised by the SIN are not new. In fact, in previous sessions of this House efforts have been made by Members to address them. However, the approach which has been adopted in the past has not necessarily been the same. Bill C-236 contains a preamble which provides the underlying rationale for the Bill. The Bill is to prevent the SIN from becoming a general use identification number and to restrict the use and disclosure of the SIN to those purposes authorized by Parliament.
Clause 2 of this Bill sets out the definition of two terms; "federal body" and "social insurance number". It is necessary to define "federal body" because, as will be revealed in future discussions, a distinction is made between entities which are federal bodies and those which are not. February 8, 1988

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS-PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE
LABOUR RELATIONS-PRINCE RUPERT GRAIN HANDLERS' STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to expand further on a question I first raised in the House on December 17, 1987. The point I want to make is the futility of strikes as well as lock-outs when a labour dispute occurs.
When a labour dispute occurs it is as a result of a breakdown in negotiations between representatives of labour and management. This was never more evident than in the recent labour dispute in Prince Rupert which began on December 9, 1987.
When operations at the Port of Prince Rupert resumed on January 22, 1988. the Canadian Wheat Board indicated that it had been unable to ship some $70 million worth of grain that would have otherwise been shipped from this port. In addition, there was some $15 million spent on transportation costs to divert grain to the St. Lawrence ports for export.
All of this has taken place while the parties involved in this dispute have both claimed to have the best interests of the western Canadian grain producers uppermost in their minds. Unfortunately, the grain producers of western Canada are the ones who suffer from the lost sales, and it is these same producers who must pay the increased transportation costs as well as the demurrage that must be paid to some of the oceangoing freighters waiting to be loaded.
Adjournment Debate
This was shameful behaviour on the part of both parties in this dispute. Both parties displayed a complete lack of concern for western grain producers. Both parties not only shirked their responsibilities but completely abdicated them. Since this facility is in large part owned by the western Canadian cooperatives which, in turn, are owned by their shareholders who by chance happen to be western Canadian grain producers, it is particularly difficult to understand how this situation could have been allowed to fester for four years before breaking out as a strike by 69 grain handlers last December 9.
The Minister of Labour of the day had appointed Mr. Vince Ready as conciliation commissioner in 1985. He worked on this problem throughout 1985 and in January, 1986, produced a report with recommendations for a settlement. This recommendation was unacceptable to the union although the companies did accept it with reservation. The dispute simmered until December 9, 1987, when the boiling point was reached.
The third party in these labour disputes is the Canadian public, who will not tolerate prolonged disruptions. The Prince Rupert situation was particularly stressful to western Canadian farmers who are already suffering from tight cash flows as a result of the cost-price squeeze. But consider also that 70 employees of CN Rail were laid off as a result of this dispute.
In my opinion, we must have a dispute settling mechanism in place that will start up at the end of a contract if the parties are not able to reach an agreement. It matters little if it is the postal workers or rail workers or the Air Canada workers, the Canadian public must have some safeguards in place. If a new contract cannot be negotiated before a present contract expires, we should have a labour court system that would automatically kick in to gear and would require both parties to submit to binding arbitration.
I further recommend that a parliamentary committee be established with all Parties represented in the House to investigate and implement this type of dispute settling mechanism.

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Gottselig) has raised a question having to do with an industrial dispute which, as we are all aware, was dealt with by this House on January 19, 1988, when it passed the Prince Rupert Grain Handling Operations Act. February 8, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The Government is fully appreciative of the frustration our Prairie grain producers experience whenever the grain handling system is threatened by a labour disruption. We are all in favour of a labour relations system in which disruption is minimized. In this regard the Government is convinced that our free collective bargaining system is the most appropriate and the most effective method of resolving labour-management conflicts in a democratic society.
Collective bargaining is an adversarial system and, as such, disputes will occur. The key to the effective functioning of this system is the acceptance by labour and management of their rights and responsibilities to settle their differences through reasonable and fair compromise.
Over the course of the tenure of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) close to 1,000 collective agreements have been negotiated under the collective bargaining provisions of the Canada Labour Code. Over this period there have been four disputes in which it was evident that labour and management could not accept their responsibility to work toward and to achieve a final, negotiated resolution of their differences.
In these instances, the parties were imposing, as a consequence of their actions, an unacceptable cost to the Canadian economy and the public interest. On each of these occasions the Government fulfilled the responsibility entrusted to it by the people of Canada by ordering an end to the disruption, prescribing a method for the final resolution of the issues in dispute.
With respect to the dispute between Prince Rupert Grain Ltd. and the grain workers union in particular, I would like to draw to the attention of all Hon. Members the fact that Mr. Justice Peter Seaton of the Court of Appeal of British Columbia has been appointed as arbitrator to resolve the three issues the parties were unable to settle.
This approach of providing the parties with every opportunity to negotiate and freely arrive at a settlement of their differences and of reserving arbitration as a remedy of last resort is far more effective in promoting constructive labour-management relations in the federal private sector.

Mr. Speaker, on March 26, 1987, I asked the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) what action he could take to remind major credit card institutions of the obligations of good corporate citizenship. Since then most banks and trust companies have lowered their rates, but not the major department stores.
They are still charging an incredible, indefensible whopping 28.8 per cent. Not only have they stayed at that line, but they have convinced at least one Minister that they charge less than banks and trust companies because they do not make a charge
for the first 30 days. They say users of their charge cards are thus better off, which is true, but only for three months.
I ask Hon. Members to sit down to figure it out. Compound the interest over a period longer than that and Hon. Members will see that after that the 2 per cent per month sky-rockets.
I can tell Hon. Members of one person in Toronto who had his indebtedness to one department store sky-rocket over a period of under two years from $2,000 to $4,000. Many people cannot pay off their accounts in shorter periods of time, so they become victimized by this massive interest rate that is afflicted upon them. I am not referring to prodigals, wastrels, or spendthrifts. I mean those people who simply have no way of coping with the situation for which they are not at fault. I am thinking of a mother, perhaps a single mother who has a group of little children to outfit for winter. Her choice is between using a charge card or letting her children go inadequately clothed through the snow. We both know what decision she makes, and what decision she should make. Very often that woman cannot pay off her indebtedness in short order.
I am thinking of a person who perhaps buys a major appliance when that person has a job and expects to have it for a reasonable length of time. Then that person finds that he or she cannot pay this sizable amount because, through no fault of their own, the plant has closed and they are out of a job. That person is not to be blamed, they cannot help it. It is not their fault if unemployment insurance is only enough for subsistence.
A profound in-depth study of this problem has shown that credit card rates chiefly cause injury to people of low income. This problem to which I refer today is not chiefly a matter of concern to yuppies, to people who have gone out and bought high ticket items and wanted to indulge themselves in a higher, faster style of life. Studies have shown that it is the type of person to whom I have just referred that is the chief victim of the abuse of interest rates on credit cards and charge cards.
I raised this question because a committee of this House, the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, in its fine, impressive, and influential report on this entire subject stated that retail stores should reduce their rates on accounts over $400. They recognized the need to draw some line such as that because there were additional administrative charges borne by department stores that were not borne by every other issuer of credit.
However, there has not been the slightest budging by the department stores. They have not moved even a tiny little inch toward acknowledging the message of this Parliament, a message of the parliamentary committee that was reinforced by a Minister of the Crown. When that report was submitted to the House, the Minister of State for Finance stated that he would act if there was not a proper response to the report of the parliamentary committee. In response to my question
February 8, 1988

raised on March 26, 1987, he stated that, if rates do not come down, as I have stated before, we will consider the best ways to proceed.
Madam Speaker, I am asking the question again. What are the best ways? I am asking, when will he proceed? When will he follow up the commitment made and implied in this question?

ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-CONVICTED MURDERER-RAPIST CHARGED WITH TRIPLE MURDERS WHILE ON PAROLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on December 13 last, a 34-year old Chilliwack woman, her 12 year old daughter, and her daughter's best friend, also 12, were murdered by the mother's common-law husband. These
Adjournment Debate
murders shocked the small, closely knit community and tragically affected the lives of family and friends of the three victims.
The murderer, Allen George Foster, of Chilliwack was a convicted murderer and rapist who had already spent seven years in jail in the early seventies for murdering an 18 year old girl, Gwen Ann Lingor. When he killed Joan Pilling, her daughter Linda Brewer, and Megan McCleary just 12 days before Christmas, he was out on full parole.
The perversity of the situation is obvious. By the very weakness of our parole system this murderer was given the freedom to murder again, not just once but three times. Had he not taken his own life on December 27 in the washroom area of the Forensic Psychiatric Institute in Port Coquitlam, he very well may have murdered yet another time. It is no wonder that my constituents in Fraser Valley East and countless other Canadians recoiled in shock and disgust at this crime but, even more so, at the system which allowed Foster to be out on our streets.
On January 18, I asked the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher) in the House why this convicted deviant sexual offender, who had committed a heinous murder and rape in 1971 and who was subsequently convicted of indecent exposure in 1986, was let out on full parole.
The Minister's response indicated that there would be a full inquest conducted by the coroner of B.C. at the end of February or March. This is welcome news to the people of B.C.
Many Members in the House of Commons voted against the motion addressing the reinstatement of capital punishment when it came up for a vote in June of last year. At the time and despite the disappointment that I felt personally, I hoped that this would force us to move in a different direction and would lead us to tightening our parole laws. We did not move fast enough for Joan Pilling, Linda Brewer, or Megan McCleary.
I realize that we have made advances in this regard with Bill C-67 from the first session, but unfortunately and obviously they were not enough. The amendments to the Parole Act and the Penitentiary Act, which received Royal Assent in July, 1986 have given us the power for the first time to keep inmates who meet the criteria under the Bill in prison for the full length of their term. I was pleased to hear that since the introduction of the Bill some 25 per cent of all people who have come before the special parole board are now being detained until the full length of their term has expired.
We have been told that the parole board followed the proper procedure before granting full parole to Foster, and I have no doubt that it did. However, human nature being what it is, is there any doubt that even if every rule was followed Foster could have stepped out of line anyway? Who can predict what a convicted murderer will do next? It is time we examined the rules.

February 8, 1988
Adjournment Debate
I would like to take the House quickly through the life of Allen George Foster from 1971 to December 27, 1987. In 1971, Foster then 20 years old, was living with a young woman in British Columbia. For reasons not known to me or probably anyone else, he decided to rape his girlfriend's 18 year old cousin, beat her to death, wrap her in chains, and throw her body into Okanagan Lake. For this crime he received a life sentence but was granted unescorted temporary absences in 1979, only seven years after the conviction.
In May 1980 the National Parole Board allowed Foster to leave custody on day parole, which meant that he had to report in only at night. One and a half years later, in October 1981, he was granted full parole. Over the years he was watched and psychiatric tests were taken, but despite these precautions he was charged in April 1986 with performing an indecent act and breaking and entering.
[DOT] <1820)
Two months later he was convicted for the indecent act and sentenced to 21 days in jail. He remained there until August of the same year. In July, 1986, he was granted day parole and in December of that year he was granted full parole. Over the next year he was closely supervised. Then, again for reasons unknown to anyone, he murdered these three innocent people in Chilliwack. The two young girls, best friends, honour students and athletes were not even born when Foster committed his first act of murder back in 1971. Unfortunately, their destinies were tied in with Foster's even then.
This case is not unique. Another convicted killer out on parole on mandatory supervision from Sumas Centre in Abbotsford did not return to the centre on September 5, 1987. He broke into an unoccupied home and stole food and household items in order to survive and then stole a vehicle belonging to the home owners. He also took a large knife. This knife was to be used by the convict just four days later to terrorize completely a Matsqui husband and wife.
The details of this crime are almost too disgusting to be repeated but will show us in even greater detail why we must do something now to tighten our parole laws. After breaking into the home while the couple was in bed, he sexually assaulted both husband and wife in front of each other, all the while threatening them with the knife. After sexually assaulting the couple, the man made them go into the kitchen and forced the wife to make him a meal. He then demanded, at gun point, that the couple give him liquor, food and other items and made them load their own car for his escape. He then drove away. This entire scene lasted three hours but will live on in the minds of this couple for the rest of their lives. The same prisoner when apprehended three hours later told the detectives "I didn't want to come out. They made me come out. I can't even make it in a backyard, let alone society or the community".
It is up to the parole system to protect society from these criminals, and I am not satisfied that this is being done. I have
written to the chairman of the Justice and Solicitor General Committee to ask that when the committee visits British Columbia it have hearings on sentencing and the parole system and that the committee visits the municipalities about which I am speaking, and Fraser Valley East. I am pleased that representatives of the three municipalities have written to the Solicitor General, as have many of the citizens. I know they will welcome the opportunity to put their cases before the committee. I am encouraging the committee to come this spring when it visits British Columbia so that people can be heard and their concerns written into the register.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-CONVICTED MURDERER-RAPIST CHARGED WITH TRIPLE MURDERS WHILE ON PAROLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I would like to express my shock and horror at the tragic death of a young mother, her daughter and a young friend in British Columbia last year. Both as Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General and as a father, I sympathize deeply with the families of these victims.
The alleged perpetrator of these crimes had been convicted of homicide 16 years earlier and was on parole at the time of these brutal murders. Two weeks later he took his own life while under psychiatric observation. We therefore may never know his full role in these crimes nor what could have motivated him.
A police investigation into the matter is now under way and the circumstances surrounding the crime will soon be examined by a coroner's inquest. Officials of the Solicitor General's ministry have been and will continue to offer whatever assistance they can to the police and coroner. In the meantime, it would be inappropriate to speculate on the findings of those inquiries.
The parolee in question was paroled after serving over 10 years of a life sentence for his earlier conviction. He had been on parole for over six years. He was seen weekly by his parole supervisor and received regular psychotherapy from two therapists. He had received psychological and psychiatric treatment throughout his sentence, including three years in the psychiatric treatment centre. By all accounts he was doing well, and at each stage of his sentence when decisions were made with regard to his very gradual release into the community, psychiatric and/or psychological opinions were considered by the parole board.
None of this can compensate for the loss of three innocent lives. The Minister will continue to examine the facts as they become known to ensure that this was the case, to learn what we can from this tragedy and to take whatever corrective action is indicated.
Our parole system must continue to help inmates to make the transition back to the community in a law-abiding fashion. At the same time the degree of risk must remain the key element in making such decisions. The harsh reality is that
February 8, 1988

assessing risk remains a matter of human judgment to a large extent and human judgment is not infallible. Despite the difficulties which will always remain, I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that this Government has done and will continue to do what it can to improve the process.
First, as Flon. Members know, Bill C-67 was passed in July of 1986. That Bill allowed the parole board to intervene and prevent the automatic release to mandatory supervision of patently dangerous inmates. Up until July 31, 1987, one year after the legislation was passed, 346 inmates had been referred to the National Parole Board for detention hearings. Of these inmates, 81 were ordered detained, subject to yearly review until sentence expiry. Seventy-two were given residency conditions, 65, one-chance mandatory supervision and 110 were released under "regular" mandatory supervision.
Second, the Parole Board is at this time implementing on a trial basis decision-making policies that will focus on undue risk. Third, the correctional service is implementing a case-
Adjournment Debate
management-strategies approach aimed at reducing and controlling the risk posed by paroled offenders.
In addition, in response to the Ruygrok inquest, certain measures such as information co-ordinators were speedily introduced and other longer-term measures have recently been proposed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Keileher) by a sentence-management review conducted by ministry officials. We are striving daily to find ways of improving our performance. To the extent the inquiries into this tragedy reveal any necessary corrective measures, they will be undertaken in addition to those to which 1 have already referred.
In closing, Madam Speaker, let me again express my deepest sympathies to the relatives and friends of those three victims who so tragically lost their lives.
